Why do instruments sound different on the same note?
opts: The blend of harmonics mixed in is different

quiz.q: Why break a complicated waveform into a sum of sine waves?
opts: Simple things are easy to handle
Sine waves are the biggest waves

light-1.title: Cover half the lens - does half the picture go?
light-1.lead: An image is not made at one point of the lens but by the whole lens together. Cover half of it and the picture is still whole.
light-1.hook: Have you ever thrown the view out of a window onto a wall with a magnifying glass? An upside-down image forms. Now what happens if you cover the bottom half of the lens with your hand? It feels as though the bottom of the picture should be cut away. It is not. Get this answer and you have how an image is made whole.

predict.q: You form an image with a convex lens and then cover half the lens. The image:
opts: Just gets dimmer all over, keeping its shape

missions: Start on the Lens screen. The object is on the left, the lens in the middle, the image on the right.
In the checkboxes on the right, turn on Focal Points (F) and Labels. The focal points on either side of the lens appear.
Set Rays at the bottom left to Principal. The three representative rays from the object are drawn.
Watch the three rays pass through the lens and meet at one point. That point is the image.
Now change Rays to Many. There are far more rays. You can see light spreading out in every direction from a single point on the object.
Do all of those rays gather at the very same point? That leads straight to the answer to ②.
Drag the object far to the left. Where does the image go and what happens to its size?
Now pull the object inside the focal point (F). The image goes and a Virtual Image appears. Tick the checkbox to see it.
Change the Focal Length handle. The thicker the lens, the closer the focal point.
Change the object to Light and drag the Screen to where the image forms.
Use the house button to visit the Mirror screen and see whether a concave mirror does the same thing.
light-1.record: When you switched Rays to "Many", where did the rays gather? And what happened when you pulled the object inside the focal point?

explain.body:
The answer is it just gets dimmer all over, keeping its shape.

What you saw on Many is the answer. Light from a single point on the object spreads in every direction and passes through every part of the lens. And the lens brings all of it back to the same single point.

So cover half the lens and the image still forms at that same point, out of the light that goes through the other half. Only half as much light arrives, so it is dimmer - that is all.

You are usually taught to find the image by drawing the three Principal rays. That is a trick to make the drawing easy, not a claim that only three rays exist. The misreading of it is what makes people think covering a lens cuts the picture.

Worth collecting what the object's position does to the image, too.

  • Beyond the focal point - a real image, upside down, forms on the far side. It can be thrown onto a screen.
  • Inside the focal point - the rays never gather; they spread. Extended backward they look as though they meet, and that is the virtual image. It is what you are looking at when a magnifying glass enlarges text.

A virtual image cannot be thrown onto a screen. No light actually gathers there; it only looks as though it does.

All of this treated light as lines travelling straight. Lenses, glasses and cameras are all explained by that picture. But some things are not, and the remaining three lessons are about those.

light-1.real: Cameras, eyes and glasses all work this way. Your lens thickening to look at something near is a way of shortening the focal length, and short-sight glasses are concave to push the focus back. It is also why telescopes are built with big lenses to see faint stars - bigger gathers more light, so the image is brighter.

quiz.q: Why do we draw only three representative rays to find an image?
opts: Because only three rays really pass through the lens
Because it is a trick to make the drawing easy
Because a lens has three parts

quiz.q: Put the object inside the focal point and:
opts: An upright virtual image is seen

quiz.q: Can a virtual image be thrown onto a screen?
opts: No - no light actually gathers there

light-2.title: Hot things change colour
light-2.lead: Heat iron and it goes red, then white. It is how we read the temperature of a star from its colour.
light-2.hook: Lesson 1 treated light only as lines travelling straight. This time you look at where light comes from. Anything with a temperature gives off light - people, stones, everything - though mostly as infrared you cannot see. Get it hot enough and it starts to be visible; get it hotter and the colour changes. Which is hotter, the red one or the blue one?

predict.q: Make an object hotter and the wavelength it gives out most strongly:
opts: Does not move; only the brightness rises
Has nothing to do with temperature

missions: The Blackbody Temperature handle on the right is the one main control in this sim.
Set the temperature low, around 3000 K. The peak of the curve sits over in the Infrared.
Raise the temperature and watch which way the peak moves. That is the answer to ②.
Find the temperature at which the peak comes inside the Visible band.
Turn on Intensity on the right for the total intensity as a number. Double the temperature - how many times bigger is the intensity?
The area under the curve is the intensity. Raise the temperature only a little and watch the area leap.
Press the Earth · Light Bulb · Sun · Sirius A buttons on the right in turn. Note the temperature and the colour of each.
Where is the peak for Earth? Does it come into the visible band?
Where is the peak for the Sun? Compare it with the range your eyes can see.
Look at the small coloured square at the top right of the screen. It tells you what colour an object at that temperature looks.
Turn on Graph Values and Labels and read the peak wavelength off exactly.
light-2.record: Write down the peak wavelength and the colour of the object at 3000 K, 5800 K and 10000 K.

explain.body:
The answer is it gets shorter - toward the blue. The hotter it is, the further the peak moves to short wavelengths.

So the colour runs in this order.

  • Low temperature - the peak is in the infrared and you cannot see it. Human bodies and the Earth are here.
  • Hotter - the peak comes into the visible and it glows red.
  • Hotter still - orange → yellow → white. The Sun (5800 K) is around here.
  • Very hot - it turns blue. Stars like Sirius A.

So a blue star is far hotter than a red one. The opposite of everyday sense, where red on a tap means hot.

What you saw under Intensity is startling too. Doubling the temperature does not double the intensity - it makes it sixteen times bigger, because it goes as the fourth power. A little more heat gives a great deal more light.

One more thing matters here. The peak moves but the curve is always continuous. Fix the temperature and how much comes out at every wavelength is completely settled. That is the exact opposite of the hydrogen spectrum in course 05, lesson 3, which was a handful of lines.

The difference matters. A single atom emits only at set wavelengths, while a hot lump of matter emits at every wavelength continuously. That is why starlight shows dark lines laid over a continuous rainbow - the continuous light from the star's surface, with the atoms outside it eating particular wavelengths out.

And the attempt to explain this smooth curve brought down the physics of a century ago. The theory of the day said the intensity should shoot to infinity at short wavelengths. To get out of it, Planck forced in the assumption that "energy only moves in lumps" - and that was the start of the quantum. The next lesson is that story.

light-2.real: Reading a star's temperature from its colour is basic astronomy. Infrared cameras finding people in the dark, thermal imaging showing how well a building is insulated, a blacksmith judging heat by the colour of iron, the "colour temperature 2700 K" on a light bulb box - all of it sits on this curve.

quiz.q: Which is hotter, a blue star or a red star?
Double the temperature and the total intensity goes to:
Why can you not see the light a human body gives off?
opts: Its peak is in the infrared

light-3.title: Some things brightness cannot buy
light-3.lead: Shine red light as hard as you like and no electron comes out. A feeble violet light and one comes straight away.
light-3.hook: At the end of lesson 2, Planck forced in the assumption that "energy only moves in lumps". It was a fudge. Then five years later, evidence that the fudge was true turned up. Shine light on a metal and electrons fly out - but in a way that simply cannot be explained if light is a wave.

predict.q: You shine red light on a metal and no electrons come out. Turn the intensity up 100 times and:
opts: Still not a single one comes out
None at first, then some after a while

missions: This is the Intro screen. The material chooser is on the left - a combo box with no label above it, showing the name of the metal - and the Intensity and Wavelength handles are at the top.
Set the metal to Sodium and put Wavelength at a long wavelength, over toward IR.
Push Intensity to the maximum. Does the Current value on the right move at all? That is the answer to ②.
Leaving the intensity at maximum, bring Wavelength slowly down toward UV. At what point do electrons suddenly start coming out?
Write down the wavelength at that point. It is this metal's threshold.
Just past the threshold, turn Intensity down. Even very faint, do electrons still come out at all?
Turn on Show Electrons and watch them fly off.
Change the metal to Copper or Platinum. Does the threshold wavelength move?
Use the house button to reach the Energy screen, where you can see how much energy the electrons come out with.
Does a shorter wavelength give the electrons more energy? What about raising the Intensity?
On the Experiment screen, measure the threshold of a Mystery metal and work out what it is.
light-3.record: Write down the wavelength at which electrons began to come out of sodium. And what changed when you raised the intensity, against what changed when you shortened the wavelength?

explain.body:
The answer is still not a single one. Brightness makes no difference whatsoever.

Treat light as a wave and this makes no sense. A wave delivers more energy the harder it hits, so even a feeble light ought to let an electron save up enough energy over time and escape. In fact, however bright and however long, nothing comes.

Instead it goes like this.

  • Wavelength longer than the threshold - not one comes out, whatever the intensity.
  • Wavelength shorter than the threshold - they come immediately, even in very faint light.
  • Raise the intensity - the number of electrons goes up. Their energy does not.
  • Shorten the wavelength further - the energy of each electron goes up.

Einstein's explanation: light is a hail of grains (photons), and the energy one grain carries is settled by the wavelength. To knock an electron loose, one grain has to carry enough energy. Weak grains are useless however many you throw.

Think of throwing balls. To knock over a brick, a ping pong ball will not do. A hundred of them will not do, nor a thousand. One baseball does it at once. Intensity is the number of balls; wavelength is the weight of each ball.

You will have seen that each metal has its own threshold, because each holds on to its electrons with a different grip. Sodium holds them loosely enough for visible light; platinum grips so hard it takes ultraviolet.

This experiment won Einstein the Nobel Prize - this, not relativity. It is the moment lesson 2's fudge turned out to be real.

light-3.real: Solar power is precisely this effect, which is why the wavelengths a panel can use decide its efficiency. Automatic door sensors, the image sensor in a digital camera, night vision goggles, and the reason ultraviolet harms skin while infrared does not - all of them come out of "the energy of one grain".

quiz.q: Raising the intensity of the light changes:
opts: The number of electrons that come out

quiz.q: Shortening the wavelength of the light:
opts: Raises the energy of each electron
Only raises the number of electrons

quiz.q: Why can this not be explained by light as a wave alone?
opts: Because a wave should work if you shine it long enough, however faint
Because a wave cannot pass through metal
Because a wave has no energy

light-4.title: Send them one at a time and the pattern still appears
light-4.lead: You throw grains one by one and a ripple pattern piles up. One grain went through both slits at once.
light-4.hook: Lesson 3 gave you the evidence that light is a grain. But there has long been evidence that light is a wave too - light through two slits overlaps and makes stripes. Natural enough, for a wave. So what if you throw the grains one at a time? One grain can only go through one slit, so there should be no pattern. This sim shows you the answer.

predict.q: You fire light one photon at a time, very slowly, through two slits. After a long while, the screen behind shows:
opts: Just two bands, at the two slit positions
Stripes - the same pattern as a wave gives

missions: This is the Experiment screen. The source is on the left, a barrier with slits in the middle, and a screen on the right.
Check that the particle chooser at the bottom left is on Photons - the buttons carry no label of their own - and set Source Intensity on the left to Max.
Leave Slit Configuration on Both Open. Stripes appear on the screen.
Now switch to Cover Left. The stripes go and one wide smear is left.
Try Cover Right as well - another single smear. Do the two smears simply added together make the stripes?
Go back to Both Open and take Source Intensity very low. Now the photons go one at a time.
Change the detection mode to Hits. A single dot is marked wherever a grain lands.
The first few land anywhere at all. Leave it running a long while. What appears as the dots pile up? That is the answer to ②.
Change the Slit Separation. What happens to the spacing of the pattern?
Change the Wavelength. Do shorter wavelengths pack the stripes closer?
Change the particle chooser at the bottom left to Electrons or Helium Atoms. Matter makes the same pattern.
Turn on Detector Left. If you check which slit it went through, what happens to the pattern?
light-4.record: What appeared as the dots piled up when you sent photons one at a time? And what happened when you watched which slit they went through?

explain.body:
The answer is stripes pile up. Sent one at a time, you still get exactly the pattern a wave gives.

Let us be clear about why that is strange.

  • Each dot lands at one place. It is a grain, all right.
  • But where it lands depends on whether both slits are open.
  • Cover one and the pattern goes, so the grain apparently knows the other slit is open.

There is no way to say it except that one grain went through both slits at once. And yet it arrives at a single point.

Remember that simply adding the two covered-slit smears did not give the stripes. So it is not "half this way, half that way". Something is overlapping, cancelling and reinforcing.

If you tried the Detector it is stranger still. The moment you check which slit it went through, the pattern vanishes. All you did was add equipment, and the result changed. Do not look and it goes both ways; look and it goes one way.

That electrons and helium atoms give the same pattern matters too. It is not only light that is odd - matter is the same. Atoms can behave like waves.

So the question this course opened with - is light a grain or a wave? - has an answer that is neither "both" nor "one of the two". It is something that is neither the grains nor the waves we know, and which looks like a grain or a wave depending on how you measure it.

That is why this counts as the most famous experiment in physics. It does not give you an answer; it shows you that the world is not shaped the way our intuition says. Course 06 picks the story up from here.

light-4.real: Electron microscopes use the wave nature of electrons: the wavelength is far shorter than light, so they see far smaller things. Semiconductor devices, quantum cryptography and quantum computers all stand on this property. The semiconductors we use every day could not be designed without this "strange" physics.

quiz.q: Send photons one at a time and the screen shows:
opts: One dot at a time, and stripes once they pile up
The whole striped pattern from the start

quiz.q: Cover one slit and the pattern:
Run the same experiment with electrons and:
opts: The same stripes as light appear

atom-1.title: What decides which element it is
atom-1.lead: Add a neutron to hydrogen and does it become helium? Exactly one thing settles the name tag.
atom-1.hook: Everything in the world is made of about a hundred elements. Yet an atom is built from only three parts - protons, neutrons and electrons. How do three parts give a hundred elements? The answer is in the numbers. But the number of which one? Get this wrong and isotopes and ions will both be a muddle later on.

predict.q: You add one neutron to a hydrogen atom (one proton). What do you get?
opts: Helium - there is one more particle

missions: There are three buckets at the bottom centre - Protons · Neutrons · Electrons. Drag particles out of them into the atom.
Put in one proton and nothing else. H lights up in the Periodic Table box on the right.
Now add one neutron. Does the name tag change? Watch the Periodic Table as you do it. That is the answer to ②.
This time add one more proton. Now the name tag does change.
Tick Element Name at the top left and the name appears in words under the atom. Handy to leave on.
Tick Neutral Atom or Ion, then take one electron away. The element is unchanged but it turns into an ion.
Tick Nuclear Stability. Keep adding neutrons and at some point it reads Unstable and the nucleus starts to shake.
Open the Net Charge and Mass Number boxes at the bottom right and watch the two numbers move independently as you add and remove particles.
Switch Model from Shells to Cloud. Two ways of drawing the same atom.
atom-1.record: Which particle changed the name tag (the element)? And which one could you add without the name tag changing?

explain.body:
The answer is still hydrogen. The name of an element is settled by the number of protons and nothing else. One proton and it is hydrogen whatever you do to it; six and it is carbon whatever you do to it.

Adding a neutron only makes it heavier. One proton plus one neutron is still hydrogen, twice as heavy as the usual kind, and we call it deuterium. Siblings like this - same proton count, different neutron count - are isotopes. They take the leading role in lesson 4.

Adding or removing electrons changes the charge and nothing else. The element stays put and it becomes an ion. It is why the Na⁺ in salt water is still sodium.

So the three parts each do a different job. Protons set the name, neutrons set the weight, electrons set the charge. Mix them up in your head and you will get stuck, guaranteed.

If Unstable appeared in the last mission, that was a trailer. However many neutrons you add the name never changes, but add too many and the nucleus cannot hold together. Lesson 4 takes that up.

atom-1.real: Carbon has six protons. Carbon-12, with six neutrons, is the usual kind; carbon-14, with eight, is mixed in rarely. Both are equally carbon, so trees and bones take them in without distinction - but only the carbon-14 fades with time. That is where dating comes from. Working out the age of an artefact begins, in the end, with "same protons, different neutrons".

quiz.q: An atom has 8 protons, 10 neutrons and 8 electrons. It is:
opts: An ion, so the element cannot be settled

quiz.q: Take one electron away and what changes?
opts: The mass number changes a lot
The charge changes - it becomes an ion

quiz.q: What is an isotope?
opts: Same number of protons, different number of neutrons
Same number of neutrons, different number of protons

atom-2.title: An atom is almost entirely empty
atom-2.lead: They fired bullets at thin gold foil and a few came straight back. Like firing a cannon at tissue paper and having it bounce.
atom-2.hook: When you built an atom in lesson 1 the screen drew the nucleus nice and big. The real proportions are nothing like that. If an atom were the size of a baseball stadium, the nucleus would be a single grain of rice at the centre. The rest is empty space. A hundred years ago nobody knew this, and they pictured an atom as raisins set in a pudding. You are about to run the experiment that destroyed that picture.

predict.q: You fire a great many alpha particles at very thin gold foil. What happens?
opts: Nearly all pass straight through, and very occasionally one bounces far off
They are all blocked and none get through

missions: Open the Plum Pudding Atom screen first. This is the model people used to believe.
Switch on the gun at the bottom to fire alpha particles. Watch how they go through - nearly all of them straight.
Under Alpha Particle on the right, run Energy from min to max. In the plum pudding, nothing you do makes much difference.
Now move to the Rutherford Atom screen. Same gun, same alpha particles.
Tick Traces. The paths stay drawn as lines and the whole picture becomes clear at a glance.
Keep firing and wait. Most go straight through, but occasionally one turns sharply or comes back. That is the answer to ②.
Under Atom on the right, take Protons from 20 up to 100. What happens to the bouncing as the nucleus gets heavier?
Take Energy to its minimum and fire again. Do slow alpha particles bend more, or less?
Check the Legend at the top of the screen for which mark is the nucleus and which is the electron energy level.
atom-2.record: Out of 100 alpha particles in the Rutherford atom, roughly how many turned sharply? And what was different from the plum pudding?

explain.body:
The answer is nearly all pass through and very occasionally one bounces far off. That is what Rutherford actually saw, and he said of it that it was about as surprising as firing a fifteen-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you.

Why surprising? The fact that nearly all pass through tells you first that the inside of an atom is nearly empty. If it were packed solid, everything would be blocked.

But the fact that one occasionally bounces far off tells you a second thing: there is something heavy and hard in there, able to turn an alpha particle right around. And something small enough that you hit it only rarely. Put the two together and only one answer survives - the mass is gathered into one tiny point. That is the nucleus.

Set against the plum pudding screen the difference is obvious. With the positive charge spread out, wherever you pass you are only nudged a little. A big bounce cannot happen. This one experiment finished the plum pudding model.

Raise the proton number and the bouncing happens more readily, because a bigger nuclear charge pushes harder. Lower the energy and slow alpha particles bend more - go past quickly and there is no time to be pushed.

atom-2.real: The method is still in use. Fire something in, look at what comes back, and work out what is inside - ultrasound scans, a bat's echolocation and airport security all share the idea. The commonest way of seeing the invisible is hitting it and counting what returns.

quiz.q: What does it tell you that nearly all the alpha particles pass through?
opts: The inside of an atom is nearly empty

quiz.q: What does it tell you that one occasionally bounces far off?
opts: The mass is gathered into one tiny point
The alpha particle is very fast

quiz.q: Why can the plum pudding model not produce a big bounce?
opts: The alpha particles are too slow
The positive charge is spread out and cannot push hard
The electrons get in the way

atom-3.title: An electron cannot be just anywhere
atom-3.lead: Why neon signs come in different colours. The light an atom gives out is not a rainbow but a handful of lines.
atom-3.hook: Lesson 2 got you as far as an atom being empty with a nucleus at the centre. So does the electron roam that empty space freely? There is a way to check: shine light on the atom and look at the light that comes back out. If an electron could be anywhere, the light coming back should be continuous, like a rainbow. Is it?

predict.q: You shine white light through hydrogen gas and look at the light coming out with a spectrometer. What do you see?
opts: Only a few lines, separated from each other

missions: Check that the switch at the top left is set to Experiment. The inside of the box is hidden behind a ? - exactly what people saw a hundred years ago.
Choose White in the light box and turn the gun on. Wait a moment and results build up in the Spectrometer below.
Count how many lines appear in the spectrometer. That is the answer to ②.
Move the switch over to Model. Now you can see inside the box, and choose between six models - Billiard Ball · Plum Pudding · Classical Solar System · Bohr · de Broglie · Schrödinger.
Work through them from Billiard Ball and find which model gives the same lines as the experiment. That search is the whole of this sim.
Choose Bohr and the electron only moves between a few fixed orbits. Compare its spectrometer against the experiment.
Change the light to Monochromatic and move the wavelength slowly. The electron only jumps at exactly the right wavelength.
Press the Transitions button at the bottom left, just under the light box. A window opens listing the steps the electron can move between - 1 ↔ 2, 2 ↔ 3 and so on.
Drop the speed at the bottom of the screen to slow and you can watch the electron jump and spit out light one event at a time.
atom-3.record: How many lines appeared in the spectrometer? And which of the six models gave the same result as the experiment?

explain.body:
The answer is only a few lines, separated from each other. Hydrogen does not give out just any colour. It gives out a few fixed wavelengths.

Why is that such a big deal? If an electron roamed the empty space freely, its energy could take any value at all, and the light coming out would run continuously through every colour. It is a few lines instead. Which means the energies an electron is allowed to have are fixed at a few values.

Run through the six models and it starts matching the experiment from Bohr onward. Billiard ball, plum pudding and classical solar system all give the wrong answer. The classical solar system is worst: the electron spirals in and is swallowed by the nucleus - if that model were right, every atom in the world would collapse instantly.

Bohr's idea is simple. An electron can only sit on fixed steps. It cannot be between them. So when an electron goes up a step and comes back down, the only light that comes out carries exactly the height of that step. A few steps means a few lines.

Monochromatic makes it clearer still. Not just any light can push an electron up. Only light that matches a step height exactly is absorbed. That is what the word quantum means - that energy only moves in lumps.

atom-3.real: Neon signs differ in colour because each gas has different step heights. The colours of fireworks, the orange of a street lamp, and working out what a star is made of from its light - all the same principle. An astronomer has never been to a star, yet reads the lines in its light and knows what it is made of. Every atom has its own fingerprint.

quiz.q: What does it mean that hydrogen gives out only a few lines?
opts: The electron's energy is fixed at a few values
The hydrogen atom is very small

quiz.q: What is fatally wrong with the classical solar system model?
opts: The electron spirals in and is swallowed by the nucleus

quiz.q: Why does an electron not jump if you set the monochromatic wavelength to just anything?
opts: Only energy that exactly matches a step height is absorbed
The electron is already at the top

atom-4.title: The moment a nucleus cannot hold
atom-4.lead: Neutrons do not change the element. But too many and the nucleus tears itself apart.
atom-4.hook: Lesson 1 settled it - adding neutrons does not change the element. So can you add as many as you like? No. Get the ratio of protons to neutrons wrong and the nucleus cannot hold together; it breaks itself apart. You are going to make that moment happen.

predict.q: Carbon has six protons. Put eight neutrons in with them and you get:
opts: Carbon, but unstable - it will decay sooner or later
A different element, since there are now more neutrons
Nothing; such a nucleus cannot be made at all

missions: On the Decay screen, set the counts with the up and down arrows for Protons and Neutrons on the left.
Set 6 protons and 6 neutrons. That is carbon-12. What does the Half-life at the top left say?
Now take the neutrons up to 8 and leave the protons at 6. That is carbon-14, and the half-life reading changes. That is the answer to ②.
Look at the Available Decays box on the right. The decays this nucleus can do appear as buttons - α decay · β⁻ decay · β⁺ decay · Proton emission · Neutron emission.
Press a button to make it decay. Watch what flies out and how the proton and neutron counts change.
The Half-Life Timescale at the top left runs from 10⁻²⁴ seconds to 10²⁴ seconds. Isotopes of the same element can have wildly different half-lives.
Keep raising the neutrons. At some point you reach Unknown, or nothing forms at all.
Watch the less stable / more stable scale and get a feel for which way you have to go to become stable.
Move to the Chart Intro screen. A nuclide chart appears with Neutron Number across and Proton Number up. The stable nuclei form a band.
Tick Magic Numbers on the chart. It marks the rows that are unusually stable.
atom-4.record: What did the half-life read for carbon-12 and for carbon-14? And how did the proton and neutron counts change when you made it decay?

explain.body:
The answer is carbon, but unstable - it will decay sooner or later. Six protons means the name is still carbon (lesson 1's rule holds). But two extra neutrons mean the nucleus cannot hold. This is carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5730 years.

Why does the ratio matter? Two forces fight inside a nucleus. Protons push each other away, being all + (the electric force from course 01). What holds them is the nuclear force, and it only reaches across very short distances. A neutron is glue: it adds nuclear force without adding any pushing.

So too few neutrons and there is not enough glue, so the pushing wins and the nucleus breaks; too many and the surplus neutrons themselves become unstable. There is a range that works, and that range is what you see as the band on the chart.

The Available Decays buttons are the tools a nucleus uses to get stable. Too many neutrons and it uses β⁻ decay to turn a neutron into a proton. Too many protons and it uses β⁺ decay. Too heavy overall and it spits out a lump by α decay. Whichever it is, the goal is the same - getting into the band.

And one more thing falls out here. If a decay changes the proton count, it changes the element. The rule you set up in lesson 1 comes back with teeth. Lesson 6 shows you that moment.

atom-4.real: Carbon-14 dating is exactly this. While something is alive it keeps taking carbon in from the air and the proportion holds; the moment it dies the supply stops and the amount halves every 5730 years. Measure what is left and you get how long ago it died. Nuclear power, radiotherapy and PET scans all start from "some nuclei are unstable".

quiz.q: A nucleus with 6 protons and 8 neutrons is which element?
opts: It is unstable, so it has no element

quiz.q: What does a neutron do in a nucleus?
opts: It is glue: nuclear force without any pushing
It holds on to the electrons

quiz.q: Which decay does a nucleus with too many neutrons usually use?
opts: β⁻ decay - it turns a neutron into a proton

atom-5.title: Nobody knows when it will break
atom-5.lead: Watch one atom with a half-life of one second for one second. The answer is "nobody knows". And yet the prediction is exact.
atom-5.hook: Lesson 4 said an unstable nucleus decays sooner or later. The word for measuring that "sooner or later" is half-life. If the half-life is one second, what happens after one second? Most people go wrong right here. And this sim is built in the order one atom → several → a great many, aimed precisely at that mistake.

predict.q: You are watching exactly one atom with a half-life of one second. After one second:
opts: It may have decayed, or it may not

missions: On the Single Atom screen, press Add Atom to put down one polonium-211 atom.
Watch Decay Time on the left and wait. When it decays, the time is printed.
Put the same atom down more than ten times. The time is different every time. That is the answer to ②.
Move the Half-life handle on the left. Changing the half-life changes the tendency of how long the decay takes.
Look at the Energy Diagram at the bottom of the screen. The alpha particle is trapped behind a wall of Potential Energy and gets out anyway - that is tunnelling.
Open the Nuclear Equation on the right: ²¹¹Po → ²⁰⁷Pb + ⁴He. The protons go down by two, so the element changes.
Move to the Multiple Atoms screen and put down several atoms. Each one is unruly - what about the group?
Move to the Decay Rate screen. Up the side is Isotope Remaining (%) and along the bottom is time. The curve is astonishingly smooth.
Look at the Half-lives scale. Every one of them takes it down to exactly half: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5.
Drag the Data Probe onto the curve and read off the percentage remaining at a particular moment.
atom-5.record: Write down five of the decay times you got from putting the same atom down again and again. And what shape was the curve on the Decay Rate screen?

explain.body:
The answer is it may have decayed, or it may not. When a single atom will decay is unknowable. Unknowable in principle - not because we have not learnt enough.

If you chose "it is half decayed" that is a very natural mistake. But a single atom cannot be half decayed. It has either decayed or it has not.

So what is a half-life? A probability. A half-life of one second means "the chance of decaying within one second is 50%". Just like a coin. You cannot say which way one coin lands, but throw ten thousand and about five thousand come up heads.

The three screens of this sim are precisely that story. On Single Atom the time differs every go and no rule shows at all. On Multiple Atoms a tendency starts to appear. On Decay Rate the curve is as smooth as if it were ruled. The one is unknowable and the whole is known exactly.

Something else that is easy to miss - atoms do not age. An atom made a moment ago and an atom a hundred million years old have exactly the same chance of decaying in the next second. Not like people at all.

What the energy diagram shows is strange too. The alpha particle is shut inside an energy wall it cannot climb, and it gets out anyway. It does not go over the wall; it goes through it. This is tunnelling, and it is the real reason decay can only ever be spoken of as a probability.

atom-5.real: Insurers and casinos live on exactly this logic. They cannot say when any one person will have an accident, yet they get the number of accidents among a hundred thousand people right. Dose calculations in radiotherapy, the fuel lifetime of a nuclear plant, and the americium-241 inside a smoke alarm all stand on half-lives.

quiz.q: One atom with a half-life of five years, after five years:
opts: Has a 50% chance of having decayed

quiz.q: 1000 atoms, half-life one hour. How many are left after two hours?
The chance of decaying in the next second, for an atom a hundred million years old against one just made:
opts: Exactly the same - atoms do not age

atom-6.title: The moment an element changes
atom-6.lead: There are no electrons in a nucleus. Yet beta decay throws one out. Where did it come from?
atom-6.hook: Alchemists gave their lives to turning lead into gold and all of them failed, because chemistry cannot do it. And yet a nucleus changes its own element. You already watched polonium become lead in lesson 5's alpha decay. This time it gets stranger. Beta decay throws an electron out of the nucleus. But as lesson 1 taught you, there are no electrons in a nucleus. How does something that is not there come out?

predict.q: In beta decay an electron flies out of the nucleus. Where did that electron come from?
opts: It was knocked out of the electron shells
It was made on the spot as a neutron turned into a proton
There were electrons inside the nucleus all along
An electron flew in from outside and bounced back out

missions: The Single Atom screen opens. The first atom put down is ³H (tritium), and you can change it to Carbon-14 under Isotope on the right.
Put an atom down and wait for it to decay. Follow with your eyes what flies out.
Open the Nuclear Equation on the right: ³H → ³He + e⁻. The mass number 3 is unchanged but the protons went up by one.
Compare the Protons and Neutrons counts before and after. Did the neutrons drop by one and the protons rise by one? That is the answer to ②.
Change Isotope to Carbon-14 - the nucleus you built in lesson 4. The carbon becomes nitrogen.
Change the Half-life and time the decay several times over. The probability from lesson 5 holds here just the same.
On the Multiple Atoms screen turn on Labels and watch which atom becomes what.
On the Decay Rate screen, check that the curve is the same shape as it was for alpha decay. Different kind of decay, same rule of half-life.
atom-6.record: How did the proton and neutron counts change across the decay? And did the mass number (protons + neutrons) change?

explain.body:
The answer is it was made on the spot as a neutron turned into a proton. Electrons are not kept in the nucleus. One is made at the instant of decay.

Here is what happens. One neutron turns into a proton plus an electron. The proton stays in the nucleus and the electron flies out. So the numbers move like this.

  • Neutrons down by one
  • Protons up by one
  • Mass number (protons + neutrons) unchanged

The charge works out as well. A neutron has charge 0, and the proton (+1) and electron (−1) it split into also add to 0. No charge was created out of nothing.

And this is where the course ties itself off. The proton count went up by one, which by lesson 1's rule means the element has changed. Tritium (1 proton) becomes helium (2), and carbon-14 (6) becomes nitrogen-14 (7). The transmutation the alchemists wanted so badly happens by itself in a nucleus.

We opened lesson 1 with "the proton count decides the element" and came back six lessons later to "that proton count changes". An atom is not an uncuttable grain but a structure whose parts get swapped out.

atom-6.real: Carbon-14 dating measures exactly this decay - counting the electrons thrown out as carbon-14 turns into nitrogen-14. A hospital PET scan uses the other direction, β⁺ decay, and spent nuclear fuel stays dangerous for a long time because beta decay runs on and on. The first step in the Sun's shining is also a β⁺ decay, a proton turning into a neutron.

quiz.q: What happens to the mass number in β⁻ decay?
Carbon-14 (6 protons) undergoes β⁻ decay and becomes:
Why does the total charge balance across β⁻ decay?
opts: Because a neutron (0) split into a proton (+1) and an electron (−1)
Because an electron came in from outside
Because charge is not conserved anyway

quantum-1.title: A covered coin and a quantum coin are not the same
quantum-1.lead: A coin under your palm has already landed. A quantum coin has not. How those two differ is the whole thing.
quantum-1.hook: You toss a coin and cover it with your palm. Heads or tails? You do not know. But there are two kinds of "do not know": already settled and I cannot see it, and not settled yet. In daily life there is no need to tell them apart - you just lift your hand. In the quantum world the two actually behave differently.

predict.q: You prepare a quantum coin with a fifty-fifty probability. Before you observe it, its state is:
opts: Already heads or tails; I simply do not know which
Neither heads nor tails, and settles into one at the moment of observation
Flicking between heads and tails very fast

missions: The left half of the screen is the Classical Coin and the right half is the Quantum "Coin". The whole layout is built to compare them side by side.
Look at the Classical Coin side first. Set Initial Orientation to the heads face.
Press Flip and then Reveal to see the result. Repeat it several times.
Put Coin Bias (State) at 0.5 for fifty-fifty, or 0.8 to get heads more often.
Now the Quantum "Coin" side. Set α and β under State to Prepare.
Make α and β equal (0.707 each). The probabilities below become 0.5 / 0.5.
Press Observe for a result. Repeat several times and check that heads and tails come out evenly.
Up to here it is indistinguishable from an ordinary coin. Judged on results alone they are the same.
Now set N = 100 under Multiple Coin Measurements and press Start.
Take 100 measurements on each side. Are the proportions the same? That is the core of ② - the results alone cannot tell them apart.
Press Reprepare and Observe several times. It is settled anew every time.
quantum-1.record: Write down the result of 100 measurements on the ordinary coin and on the quantum coin. Looking at the two results, could you tell which was which?

explain.body:
The answer is neither heads nor tails, and it settles into one at the moment of observation.

And yet, as the screen showed you, the results alone cannot tell them apart. A hundred measurements or ten thousand, both come out even. So on what grounds do we say they differ?

The difference lies in what you can do before you measure. Think back to the two-slit experiment in course 04, lesson 4.

  • If it were already settled - the grain went through the left slit or the right one, and you should get the sum of the two smears.
  • If it is not settled - the two possibilities overlap, cancelling and reinforcing, and make stripes.

What actually came out was stripes. So it is not "it was settled and we merely did not know".

This state is called superposition. It is often described as "both at once", which is not quite right. It is a third state that is neither heads nor tails, and we stretch ordinary words over it because there is no everyday word for it.

α and β on screen are how that state is written down. Square them and you get each probability. The important part is that α and β carry more information than the probabilities do. Two states that look identical in probability can differ in α and β, and that difference is what shows up in the two-slit experiment.

If you chose "flicking very fast", that is a very natural thought. But it also means settled into one at every instant, so in the end it is the same as the first option.

quantum-1.real: Quantum computers use this property. A bit in an ordinary computer is 0 or 1, while a quantum bit can be left in superposition, so for certain problems it reaches an answer in far fewer steps. Quantum cryptography spots eavesdropping the same way, using "measuring it changes the state".

quiz.q: The state of an ordinary coin you have covered up:
opts: Is already settled; I simply do not know it

quiz.q: Can you tell a quantum coin from an ordinary one by the measurement results alone?
opts: No - it takes a different experiment
Yes, if you take enough measurements

quiz.q: Then where does the evidence that they differ come from?
opts: Take enough measurements and the proportions come apart
The overlap before measurement shows up as stripes in the two-slit experiment
A quantum coin lands the same face every time

quantum-2.title: Measuring it changes it
quantum-2.lead: Put a thermometer in soup and the soup cools a little. In quantum mechanics it is worse than that - before you measure, there is no value at all.
quantum-2.hook: Lesson 1 said a quantum coin settles when you observe it. So what is observation doing? This sim tells the same story with the polarization of light instead of a coin. Polarization is something you can actually hold, so it is far more concrete. And here something genuinely strange turns up - change the order you measure in and the result changes.

predict.q: Light has passed a filter that only lets vertical polarization through. Now you hold up a horizontal filter:

missions: The Coins screen repeats what lesson 1 covered. Worth one more look if any of it did not land.
Use the house button to reach the Photons screen. The source is on the left, the Polarizing Beam Splitter in the middle, and the Polarization Detectors on the right.
Set Photon Polarization Angle at the bottom left to Vertical (V).
Leave it on Single Photon and send photons one at a time. Which detector responds? Is it always the same one?
Now change the angle to 45°. Which way it goes is now unpredictable.
Switch to Many Photons and send a lot. Check that at 45° the split is even.
Under Behavior, switch between Classical and Quantum. The classical model splits the light and sends both ways; the quantum one sends it whole, one way.
That difference matters. A single photon is not divided in half. It goes one way, entire.
Change the light to Unpolarized. What does light with no set direction do at the splitter?
Use the house button to reach the Spin screen for the same story told with the spin of an electron.
On the Spin screen, put several measuring devices in a row at different angles. What you measured earlier gets erased by what you measure later.
quantum-2.record: At a polarization angle of 45°, which way did each individual photon go? And what was the proportion when you sent many?

explain.body:
The answer is none of it gets through. Take light that is purely vertical, hold up a horizontal filter, and it is blocked completely.

So far a wave picture explains it. But what this sim showed you is far stranger.

Think back to sending a single photon polarized at 45° into a vertical/horizontal splitter. That photon is neither vertical nor horizontal. And yet it arrived at one detector, whole. It did not split in half.

Switching Behavior to Classical made the contrast nicely. The classical model treats light as a wave, so it divides the intensity and sends both ways. Reality (quantum) does not. One grain does not divide, and which way it goes is settled only by probability.

And once through, that photon is no longer at 45°. It has become the direction you measured. The information that it was at 45° is gone.

That is what "measurement changes the state" means. It is not like a thermometer cooling the soup a little. That nudges a value that was already there; here there was no such value before the measurement and the measurement makes one.

If you chained devices on the Spin screen it is clearer still. Measure vertically, then horizontally, then vertically again, and the first vertical result has been erased. The act of measuring horizontally destroyed the vertical information. The order you measure in changes the result.

This is exactly the story behind course 04, lesson 4, where the pattern vanished once you checked which slit. It looked bizarre then; once you know measurement changes the state, it is the obvious outcome.

quantum-2.real: Sunglasses and camera filters use polarization. An LCD screen is liquid crystal between two polarizers, opening and closing the light. Quantum cryptography catches eavesdroppers on this principle - the moment an eavesdropper measures the signal, the state changes and leaves a trace. Security guaranteed by a law of physics.

quiz.q: One photon polarized at 45° meets a vertical/horizontal splitter:
opts: It divides in half and goes both ways
It goes one way whole, and which way is a matter of probability

quiz.q: After the measurement, that photon's polarization is:
opts: Changed to the direction you measured

quiz.q: Measure vertical → horizontal → vertical and:
opts: The first vertical result comes back unchanged
Measuring horizontally erased the vertical information
No result comes out at all

quantum-3.title: Confine it and the energy becomes a staircase
quantum-3.lead: A free particle can have any energy at all. Confine it and only fixed values are left.
quantum-3.hook: Course 05 said an electron can only sit on fixed steps. Why steps of all things? We let it go as "apparently so" back then; now it can be answered. The answer is in the waves of course 04. In course 03 you saw a guitar string refuse to make just any note and give only fixed notes. A confined wave cannot take just any shape. That is all there is to it.

predict.q: Confine an electron in a narrow box and the energies it can have are:

missions: This is the One Well screen. The upper graph is the Energy Diagram and the lower one is the Wave Function.
Check that the well shape on the right is Infinite Square - a box with very high walls.
The upper graph shows several horizontal lines. Those are the energies the electron can have. Is there anything between them? That is the answer to ②.
Press a line to select E₁. The wave for that state is drawn below.
Go up through E₂ · E₃ and watch how the number of humps grows.
Think back to the guitar string in course 03. Are these not the same shapes a string fixed at both ends can make?
Choose Probability Density at the bottom right. It shows you where the electron is likely to be found.
At E₁ the middle is highest; at E₂ the middle is 0. There is a place the electron is never found at all.
Drag the width handle to make the box narrower. What happens to the spacing of the steps?
And wider? The steps pack together. Widen it a great deal and they look almost continuous.
Change the well shape to Coulomb. This is the situation of the hydrogen atom from course 05.
quantum-3.record: Write down the wave shape and the number of humps for E₁, E₂ and E₃. And what happened to the step spacing when you narrowed the box and when you widened it?

explain.body:
The answer is only a few fixed values. The horizontal lines in the upper graph are those values, and the energies between the lines cannot be had.

Why? The answer is in a confined wave.

Think of the guitar string from course 03. Both ends are fixed, so not just any wavelength will do. Only wavelengths that come out even at both ends survive; the rest cancel themselves out. That is why a guitar string gives fixed notes.

An electron is the same. Course 04 showed you that electrons behave like waves. Confine that wave in a box and only the shapes that come out even at both ends survive. Each shape has its own energy, so the energies are fixed at a few values too.

That is exactly what you saw on screen. E₁ has one hump, E₂ two, E₃ three - the same shapes as the harmonics of a guitar string.

Changing the width of the box is the high point of this lesson.

  • Narrower - the steps get further apart. The tighter the confinement, the more the values jump.
  • Wider - the steps pack together. Widen it a great deal and they look almost continuous.

Which is why you never see quantum effects day to day. The things we handle are so large that the steps are infinitely fine, and that is indistinguishable from "any value at all". Quantum only shows itself when things are small.

Switching to Coulomb gives you the hydrogen atom from course 05, lesson 3. What was stated there - "an electron only sits on fixed steps" - now has its why: the nucleus is confining the electron, and a confined wave has only a few possible shapes.

Remember what Probability Density showed as well. At E₂ the electron is never found in the middle of the box. And yet it is found on both sides. How did it cross without passing through the middle? There is no good answer to that question - because an electron is not a grain that travels in the first place.

quantum-3.real: Semiconductors work on this principle. The colour of an LED is set by the height of the step an electron drops down, and lasers use transitions between fixed levels too. A quantum dot display (QLED) changes the size of its grains to tune the step spacing and so make its colours - exactly what you did by changing the width of the box in this lesson.

quiz.q: Why does a confined electron have only fixed energies?
opts: Because a confined wave has only a few possible shapes
Because there is not enough energy

quiz.q: Narrow the box and the energy steps:
Why are quantum effects invisible in everyday life?
opts: Because things are large, so the steps are extremely fine
Because quantum laws do not apply to large objects
Because our eyes are not good enough

space-1.title: The Moon is falling right now
space-1.lead: Being in orbit is really a matter of falling continuously and missing continuously.
space-1.hook: In course 02, a ball thrown sideways hit the ground at the same moment as one simply dropped. So what if you throw it very, very hard? It goes further. Harder still, further still. But the Earth is round. What if the ground curves away below just as fast as the ball falls? The ball never reaches the ground and goes round the Earth instead. That is an orbit.

predict.q: While the Moon is going round the Earth, gravity suddenly disappears. What does the Moon do?
opts: Flies off in a straight line, the way it was going at that moment

missions: Start on the Model screen. At the bottom right you can choose combinations like a star with a planet, or the Earth with the Moon - the buttons are pictures of the bodies.
In the checkboxes on the right turn on Velocity, Path and Grid. The arrows and the trail appear.
Press play and let it go round a few times. The Path draws itself.
Look at the Velocity arrow on the planet. It always points along the tangent of the orbit - never at the centre.
Now switch Gravity on the right to off. What happens? That is the answer to ②.
Put it back to on and use Return Objects to go back to the start.
Drag the planet's velocity arrow to make the speed smaller. What happens to the orbit?
Now make it much larger. The planet leaves the orbit and flies away.
Hunt for the speed that makes the orbit very nearly a circle. Too slow will not do and neither will too fast.
Raise the Star Mass. Same speed - how does the orbit change?
Use the house button to visit the To Scale screen. Drawn at true proportions, you can barely see anything. It tells you how empty space is.
space-1.record: What path did the planet take when you turned gravity off? And what happened to the orbit when you made the speed smaller, and larger?

explain.body:
The answer is it flies off in a straight line, the way it was going. With gravity off on screen, the planet will have left in a straight line.

Why straight? With no force on it, an object keeps going the way it was going. The Moon is trying to go straight this very moment, and gravity keeps bending it inward.

So an orbit is this picture.

  • The Moon moves fast sideways
  • Gravity keeps pulling it toward the Earth
  • The Moon keeps falling, but it is going sideways fast enough to miss the Earth

So the Moon is falling right now. Its sideways speed is simply right for it to keep missing forever. Astronauts float in a space station not because there is no gravity but because they are falling along with the station.

Worth collecting what changing the speed showed you.

  • Too slow - it does not miss by enough and spirals inward.
  • Too fast - gravity cannot hold it and it flies away.
  • Just right - a stable orbit.

Which is why speed matters more than height when you launch a satellite. Lift it high and it just falls back. You have to push it fast enough sideways to reach orbit.

Remember, too, that you could see almost nothing on the To Scale screen. Every textbook diagram is exaggerated. Space is far emptier than the pictures.

space-1.real: GPS satellites, communications satellites and the space station are all in the state of falling continuously and missing continuously. A geostationary satellite appears to hang at one spot in the sky because its period matches the rotation of the Earth. A SpaceX rocket tips over sideways after launch for the same reason - it is buying sideways speed, not height.

quiz.q: Which way does the velocity arrow of an orbiting planet point?
opts: Always along the tangent of the orbit

quiz.q: If a satellite is going too fast:
opts: It leaves the orbit and flies away
It carries on as it was

quiz.q: Why do astronauts on a space station float?
opts: Because there is no gravity up there

space-2.title: The Sun wobbles too
space-2.lead: The Sun pulls the planet and the planet pulls the Sun. So the Sun cannot stay still.
space-2.hook: In lesson 1 the star stayed put and only the planet went round. But does it? Course 01 said two charges pull each other with forces of equal size. Gravity is the same. The Sun pulls the Earth, and the Earth pulls the Sun by just as much. So the Sun ought to move as well. In this sim you lay out the bodies yourself and watch that wobble.

predict.q: Compare the force with which the Sun pulls the Earth against the force with which the Earth pulls the Sun:
opts: They are the same size - only the directions differ
They differ by the ratio of the masses

missions: Start on the Intro screen. One star and one planet are laid out.
In the checkboxes on the right turn on Gravity Force, Path and Grid. The force arrows appear.
Compare the length of the Gravity Force arrows on the two bodies. Which is longer? That is the answer to ②.
Press play and let it run. Does the star move at all? If it is hard to see, go on to the next mission.
Use Mass at the bottom left to reduce the mass of the star. Now it wobbles far more.
Turn on Center of Mass on the right. You can see the two bodies going round with that point between them.
Turn on Follow Center of Mass and the view locks onto that point.
Make the two masses nearly equal. Where does the centre of mass go?
Use the house button to reach the Lab screen, where you can take Bodies up to three or more.
Put down three bodies and press play. Does the orbit settle? Try it a few times.
Use the zoom control to chase down a body that has flown off.
space-2.record: How did the lengths of the two gravity force arrows compare? And how did the star's motion change when you reduced its mass?

explain.body:
The answer is they are the same size. The two arrows on screen will have been the same length, pointing opposite ways.

It was the same with the two charges in course 01, lesson 3. However large you made one charge, both figures pulled with the same force. Gravity works the same way. Forces always come in pairs, equal in size, opposite in direction.

So why does only the Earth appear to go round? Because the forces are equal but the masses are not. Under the same force, the heavier one moves less. The Sun is 330,000 times heavier than the Earth, so it moves 330,000 times less.

The Sun therefore does move - just very little. Reducing the star's mass on screen and watching the wobble grow is the proof.

The centre of mass is the heart of this story. The two bodies do not orbit each other; they both go round one shared point. That point is the centre of mass, and it sits far closer to the heavy one. For the Sun and the Earth it lies inside the Sun, which is why the Sun looks as though it turns slightly on the spot.

Make the two masses similar and the centre of mass moves toward the middle, giving you a binary star with the two going round each other. Space is full of them.

With three bodies the orbit will not have settled easily. This is the famous three-body problem. With two the answer comes out cleanly; with three there is no general solution. Nudge it slightly and you get a completely different result.

space-2.real: One of the ways we find planets around other stars is exactly this - watching for a tiny wobble in the star. The planet is never seen directly; its existence is deduced from the star's wobble. A good share of the thousands of exoplanets found so far were found this way.

quiz.q: The force with which the Earth pulls the Sun is:
opts: The same as the force with which the Sun pulls the Earth

quiz.q: So why does the Sun barely move?
opts: It is far heavier, so it moves less under the same force

quiz.q: What do two bodies really go round?
opts: The centre of the heavier one
The centre of mass of the two
The centre of the lighter one

space-3.title: It speeds up when it is close
space-3.lead: An orbit is not a perfect circle but a squashed ellipse. So the speed differs through the year.
space-3.hook: Textbook pictures of the solar system draw the planets on neat circles. They are really slightly squashed ellipses. Which means there is a near point and a far point from the star. So what about the speed? Lesson 1 said too fast and it flies away, too slow and it spirals in. That rule works within a single orbit too.

predict.q: Where in an elliptical orbit is a planet fastest?

missions: Start on the First Law screen. The controls are all on the right. There is no handle for the shape of the orbit - you change it by dragging the planet or the velocity arrow (v) attached to it.
Tick Eccentricity on the right. A scale from 0 to 1 appears on the left with the current value marked. Drag the planet to bring the value close to 0 for a circle, or raise it for a long thin ellipse.
That scale is marked with Mercury · Earth · Eris · Nereid · Halley. They are there to compare against, not to choose - drag your orbit until it sits next to Halley.
In the checkboxes on the right turn on Velocity and Speed. You get the arrow and the number.
Leave the eccentricity high and press play. Note the speed reading close to the star and far from it. That is the answer to ②.
Turn on Axes and Foci to see the skeleton of the ellipse. The star sits at a focus, not at the centre.
Use the house button to reach the Second Law screen. Period Divisions sets how many pieces the orbit is cut into.
Press play and the wedges fill in one at a time. Turn on Area Values and compare the areas of the pieces.
The wedge near the star is short and fat; the far one is long and thin. But what about the areas?
Go to the Third Law screen for the Period vs Semi-major Axis graph.
Set the axes to T² and a³. Do the points fall on a straight line? What about other combinations?
space-3.record: Write down the speed close in and far out. And what were the areas of the wedges on the Second Law screen?

explain.body:
The answer is at its closest to the star. Closer is faster, further is slower.

There are two ways to say why.

First, gravity is stronger there. The closer it is the harder the pull, so it is dragged along faster. As with the Coulomb force in course 01, the force rises sharply as the distance closes.

Second, the energy trade. On the skate park in course 02, losing height gained you speed. An orbit is the same. Coming close to the star is "going down" and gains speed; moving away is "going up" and loses it. The same picture as a roller coaster.

The Second Law is that turned into an exact rule. The wedges will all have had the same area. Close in the radius is short, so it has to sweep quickly to make the same area; far out the radius is long, so sweeping slowly is enough. "It sweeps equal areas in equal times" - that is Kepler's second law.

You will have checked the Third Law too. The points only fall on a straight line when the axes are T² and a³. So the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the size of the orbit. Which is why a planet further out takes so much longer to go round - Neptune takes 165 years.

That the star sits at a focus of the ellipse, not at its centre, matters as well. That is the first law, and it is what creates a near side and a far side. The Earth is closest to the Sun in January - the seasons are made by tilt, not by distance.

space-3.real: Comets are a good example. Halley's comet has such a high eccentricity that it tears past near the Sun and crawls for decades out at the far end. Designing satellite orbits, working out when a Mars probe should depart, and predicting when an asteroid comes near the Earth are all calculated with these three laws.

quiz.q: Where in an elliptical orbit is a planet slowest?
opts: At its closest to the star
At its furthest from the star

quiz.q: What does Kepler's second law say?
opts: It sweeps equal areas in equal times
It covers equal distances in equal times

matter-1.title: Ice and water are the same grains
matter-1.lead: Solid, liquid and gas are not different substances. They are the same grains, shaking harder or less hard.
matter-1.hook: Ice, water and steam look nothing like one another. Hard, flowing, invisible. And yet every single grain is exactly the same water molecule. So what is different? This sim magnifies down to the grains and shows you the answer. And what temperature really is falls out along the way.

predict.q: You warm a solid until it becomes a liquid. What has changed about one grain?
opts: The grain has turned into a different kind

missions: Start on the States screen.
Choose Neon under Atoms & Molecules on the right. Simple grains are easier to watch.
Press the Solid button on the right. The grains line up in rows and shiver in place.
Push the handle at the bottom toward Heat and warm it slowly. The Temperature at the top left goes up.
How do the grains change? Do they get bigger, or do they shake faster? That is the answer to ②.
Keep heating and the rows collapse into a Liquid. Do the grains stay in contact while changing places?
Heat further and it becomes a Gas. Now the grains are far apart and fly about at random.
Now push toward Cool and chill it. Does it go back?
Change to Water and do the same. Can you see the grains arranging themselves more loosely as it freezes?
Use the house button to reach the Phase Changes screen, where you can also apply Pressure. Raise the pressure to turn the gas into a liquid.
On the Interaction screen, change the Distance Between Atoms. Close in it is Repulsive; far out it is Attractive.
matter-1.record: As you heated it from solid to gas, what happened to the size of the grains and to their shaking?

explain.body:
The answer is they shake faster. The grains themselves change neither size nor kind.

Collecting what you saw on screen:

  • Solid - the grains line up in rows and only shiver in place. The force holding them together beats the shaking.
  • Liquid - still in contact, but changing places. Which is why it flows.
  • Gas - apart from each other, flying about at random. The shaking has beaten the holding.

So the three states are a matter of which way the contest between holding and shaking has tipped. The grains are the same throughout.

And here is what temperature is. Temperature is not a degree of hotness but how fast the grains are moving. Heating something is shaking its grains harder.

Freezing water is the interesting one. Most substances pack tighter as they freeze; water arranges itself more loosely. Which is why ice floats. Thanks to that odd property, a lake freezes from the surface down and the life in it gets through the winter.

What you saw on the Interaction screen matters too. Grains pull when far apart and push when close. So they settle at a particular distance. It is why a solid has a volume at all, and why there is a limit to how far you can squeeze anything.

matter-1.real: All of cooking is this story. Water boiling and then sitting at 100 °C, a pressure cooker cooking at a higher temperature, dry ice going straight to gas without a liquid stage - all contests between grains. Without ice floating, lakes would freeze from the bottom every winter and the fish would not survive.

quiz.q: Warm some water and one water molecule:
What does temperature represent?
opts: How fast the grains are moving
