matter-2.title: Pressure is grains hitting the wall
matter-2.lead: A balloon swells not because something inside is pushing, but because grains are drumming on the wall without a pause.
matter-2.hook: Lesson 1 said the grains of a gas fly about at random. So what is pressure? People wave at it with "the air pushes out", but at the level of grains it is far simpler. Grains hitting the wall is all it is. This sim even has a Collision Counter, so you can count the drumming yourself.

predict.q: Gas in a sealed container. You hold the volume and double the temperature. The pressure:
opts: Goes up - the grains hit harder and more often
Depends on the number of grains

missions: This is the Ideal screen. Press the pump on the left to put gas into the container.
Check the Pressure gauge at the top and the Temperature readout on the left.
Under Hold Constant on the right, choose Volume (V). The volume is now fixed.
Push the handle at the bottom toward Heat. What does the Pressure do as the temperature rises? That is the answer to ②.
Turn on the Collision Counter on the right. It reports Wall Collisions. Do they rise as you heat?
Now switch Hold Constant to Temperature (T) and push the right-hand wall of the container inward to reduce the volume. The pressure?
Set it to Nothing and heat the container: the lid is pushed up. The volume grew.
Under Particles on the left, put in the same number of Heavy and Light ones.
Which fly about faster, the heavy grains or the light ones?
Use the house button to reach the Diffusion screen and remove the divider in the middle. The two gases mix by themselves.
On the Energy screen, look at the speed distribution of the grains. They are not all at one speed - they are all over the place.
matter-2.record: With the volume held, what happened to the pressure and to the wall collision count as you heated it? And how did the speeds of the heavy and light grains compare?

explain.body:
The answer is it goes up. The number on the Collision Counter rising alongside is the proof.

Start with what pressure is. Pressure is grains drumming on the wall. So two things raise it.

  • The grains hit more often, or
  • each hit lands harder

Raise the temperature and the grains speed up, so both go up. That is why the pressure climbs so sharply.

The pressure also rose when you reduced the volume. This time the grains kept their speed but the walls came closer, so they hit more often.

To collect it:

  • Temperature ↑ (volume held) → pressure ↑ - harder and more often
  • Volume ↓ (temperature held) → pressure ↑ - closer walls, more often
  • Number of grains ↑ → pressure ↑ - more things doing the hitting

Every gas law in the textbook comes out of this one picture. There is no separate formula to memorise.

That the heavy grains were slower matters too. The same temperature means the same energy, and with the same energy a heavier thing moves more slowly. It is why a helium balloon goes down faster than an air-filled one, and why perfume takes time to fill a room.

Remember, too, that the speeds on the Energy screen were all different. Temperature is only an average, and the few unusually fast ones escaping from the surface of a liquid are what evaporation is. It is why washing dries without boiling.

matter-2.real: Filling a tyre and getting a pressure warning light in winter, a pressure cooker taking water past 100 °C, why you must not put an aerosol can in a fire, a crisp packet swelling as a plane takes off - all of it comes from this one picture.

quiz.q: The pressure of a gas is:
opts: How much the grains drum on the wall

quiz.q: Hold the temperature and reduce the volume. The pressure:
At the same temperature, a heavier grain is:

matter-3.title: Why is water bent?
matter-3.lead: Two bonds ought to make a straight line, and yet water is bent. It is because of electron pairs you cannot see.
matter-3.hook: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a straight line while water (H₂O) is bent. Both have one central atom with two arms on it. Why the difference? The answer is in what you cannot see. And this difference in shape leads straight into the next lesson - why water is so special.

predict.q: A central atom has 2 bonds. But it also has 2 lone pairs that take no part in bonding. The shape is:
opts: Only the bonds matter, so the lone pairs make no difference

missions: Start on the Model screen. One central atom is laid out, and you attach arms from the right.
Under Bonding on the right, attach two single bonds. What shape do you get?
Turn on Name at the bottom left and it reads Linear. A straight line.
Now attach one Lone Pair. Does the shape change?
Attach one more lone pair. Now you have 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. This is the structure of water, and the answer to ②.
Turn on Show Bond Angles on the right. The angle appears as a number. How many degrees?
Turn Show Lone Pairs off and on. With it off, you cannot see why it is bent.
Now take the bonds up to 3 and 4. What shape does each give?
With 4 bonds, check that the angle is not 90°. Why not?
Use the house button to reach the Real Molecules screen, where you can pick real molecules like H₂O · CO₂ · NH₃ · CH₄.
Flip between CO₂ and H₂O and compare the number of lone pairs.
matter-3.record: Write down the shape and the angle with 2 bonds alone, and with 2 bonds plus 2 lone pairs.

explain.body:
The answer is bent. That is exactly water's structure, and the angle is about 104.5°.

The reason is simple. Electron pairs push each other away. They are all negative. So the pairs move to wherever they are as far from each other as possible.

The important part is that a pair used in a bond and a pair that is not push exactly the same. So when you work out the shape you have to count both.

  • 2 pairs → opposite each other → linear (180°)
  • 3 pairs → triangular
  • 4 pairs → tetrahedral (about 109.5°)

Water has 2 bonds plus 2 lone pairs = 4 pairs in all, so they spread tetrahedrally. But all we can see is the two bonds, so it looks bent.

Turning Show Lone Pairs off was a good check. With it off there is no telling why it bends. Something invisible is setting the shape.

Carbon dioxide is straight for the same reason. The central carbon has no lone pairs, so only the two bonds push apart, and that gives 180°.

Remember also that with 4 bonds the angle was 109.5°, not 90°. Drawn on paper it looks like a cross, so 90° feels right; but it is really three-dimensional, and spreading into a tetrahedron gets them furthest apart. Molecules are not flat.

This difference in shape is where the next lesson starts, because the same bonds give a whole molecule with different properties depending on the shape.

matter-3.real: How a drug works in the body hangs on this shape, because an enzyme and a drug molecule have to fit like a lock and a key. Built of the same atoms, a different order and angle makes a completely different substance. The thalidomide disaster of the 1960s is usually given as the example, though the real story is a step more complicated - the two mirror images convert into each other in the body, so feeding only the safe one would not have prevented it.

quiz.q: What sets the shape of a molecule?
opts: The count of bonds and lone pairs together

quiz.q: Why is CO₂ a straight line?
opts: Because the central atom has no lone pairs

quiz.q: With 4 electron pairs, why is the angle not 90°?
opts: Spreading into a tetrahedron in three dimensions gets them furthest apart

matter-4.title: Shape changes the properties
matter-4.lead: Even when every bond is lopsided, a symmetric shape cancels them out. It is why water is special.
matter-4.hook: Lesson 3 said water is bent and carbon dioxide is straight. Yet water dissolves almost anything and carbon dioxide barely dissolves in it - though both have bonds where oxygen pulls hard on the electrons. The difference is in the shape. And this story uses adding vectors from course 02 exactly as it stands.

predict.q: Two bonds are each lopsided to one side. When is the whole molecule not lopsided?
opts: If the bonds are lopsided the molecule always is
If the two bonds point exactly opposite ways they cancel out
They cancel if the atoms are heavy

missions: Start on the Two Atoms screen. Two atoms joined by one bond.
The Electronegativity handles for Atom A and Atom B below are how hard each pulls on the electrons.
Set the two equal. Turn on Bond Dipole on the right and the arrow disappears - there is no lopsidedness.
Now raise Atom B alone to its maximum. The arrow points toward B. The electrons have shifted that way.
Turn on Partial Charges and δ+ and δ− appear - slightly positive and slightly negative.
Turn on Electric Field. A lopsided molecule turns to face the field.
Use the house button to reach the Three Atoms screen. Three atoms now, and you can change the shape.
Turn on both Bond Dipoles and Molecular Dipole. Two small arrows and one big one appear.
Drag A and C to straighten the molecule into a line. The bond arrows are still there - what happens to the molecular arrow? That is the answer to ②.
Now bend it back. The molecular arrow reappears.
On the Real Molecules screen, pick H₂O and CO₂ and compare. The difference in shape from lesson 3 becomes a difference in properties here.
matter-4.record: What did the molecular dipole arrow do when you straightened the three atoms into a line, and when you bent them?

explain.body:
The answer is if the two bonds point exactly opposite ways they cancel. On screen, straightening the molecule left the bond arrows exactly as they were while the molecular arrow disappeared.

Course 02, lesson 4 said that adding vectors of size 3 and 4 gives anything from 1 to 7 depending on direction. The same thing happens here. A bond dipole is an arrow with a size and a direction, and the lopsidedness of the whole molecule is those arrows added up.

  • Straight (symmetric) - the two arrows are exactly opposite → the sum is 0 → non-polar
  • Bent - the two arrows are at an angle → the sum is not 0 → polar

So a molecule can be un-lopsided even when its bonds are lopsided, as long as the shape is symmetric.

Carbon dioxide is exactly that case. Each C=O bond is strongly lopsided, but being straight they cancel. Water is bent, so nothing cancels and the whole thing is lopsided - a polar molecule.

That difference has enormous consequences.

  • Water dissolves almost anything. Lopsided ends grab each other, so it can tear apart an ionic substance like salt.
  • Water grabs other water hard. Its boiling point is far above that of molecules of similar size. Water being liquid at room temperature at all is down to this.
  • Oil does not mix. Being non-polar, it has no way to grab hold of water.

Lesson 1 said the force with which grains hold each other settles the state. What settles the strength of that holding is exactly this lopsidedness. The course closes its loop here - shape sets the lopsidedness, the lopsidedness sets the holding force, and that force sets solid, liquid and gas.

matter-4.real: "Oil and water do not mix" is the whole of this story. Detergent lifts grease because one end of the molecule is polar and the other is not, so it can grab both. A microwave heating only the water, soap washing your hands, waterproofing on a coat, how well a drug is absorbed - all of it divides along polarity.

quiz.q: Why is CO₂ non-polar?
opts: It is straight, so the two lopsidednesses cancel

quiz.q: Why is H₂O polar?
opts: It is bent, so nothing cancels

quiz.q: Why does oil not mix with water?
opts: It is non-polar, so it has no way to grab hold of water

mix-1.title: One step of pH is ten times
mix-1.lead: pH 2 and pH 3 look one step apart. They are ten times apart.
mix-1.hook: Lemon juice is about pH 2 and coffee about pH 5. Three apart in numbers, so it is easy to think it is about three times as sour. It is really a thousand times. The pH scale is not like an ordinary ruler: one step is a multiplication by 10. There is a reason for a scale like that, and knowing it also clears up the common belief that "adding water makes it neutral".

predict.q: You take an acid at pH 2 and add water until the total volume is 10 times as much. The pH is:
opts: 7 - you added water, so it is neutral

missions: This is the Macro screen. The dropper above the beaker in the middle lets you pour a liquid in.
Choose Orange Juice from the list on the right and press the dropper to pour it into the beaker.
Drag the pH meter on the left into the liquid. A pH value appears. Write it down.
Open the Water tap at the top right and pour water in. Which way does the pH move?
Keep pouring until the beaker is full. Does the pH go past 7? That is the core of ②.
Open the drain below to empty it, then do the same thing with Drain Cleaner (a base).
Check where Acidic · Neutral · Basic sit on the scale at the left.
Pick several liquids and note their pH - Battery Acid · Coffee · Milk · Spit · Hand Soap.
Use the house button to reach the Micro screen, where you can see the number of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ particles in the same liquid. The lower the pH, which of them is more plentiful?
mix-1.record: How far did the pH go as you kept pouring water into the orange juice? And did it pass 7?

explain.body:
The answer is 3. Dilute it ten-fold with water and the pH rises by exactly 1.

Why 1? pH reports how many hydrogen ions (H₃O⁺) there are, and it writes that count as a power of ten. pH 2 means there is "10⁻²" of it, pH 3 means "10⁻³". Dilute ten-fold and the count becomes a tenth, so the exponent moves one and the pH goes up by 1.

So one step of pH = ten times. Lemon juice (pH 2) and coffee (pH 5) are 3 apart, which is 10 × 10 × 10 = a thousand times. A log scale is what you build to fit a difference that large on one line. It is the same device as the half-life scale in course 05, where one step was a thousand times.

If you chose "it becomes 7", that is a very common belief. Adding water brings the pH toward 7 but never past it. No amount of water turns an acid into a base. Filling the beaker on screen without ever passing 7 is the proof.

Diluting and neutralising are different things. Diluting is adding water to make it weaker; neutralising is adding the opposite (a base) to remove the property itself.

Collect what the Micro screen showed you too. Acidic means plenty of H₃O⁺; basic means plenty of OH⁻. pH is in the end just those two counts squeezed into a single number.

mix-1.real: Stomach acid is pH 1-2, strong enough to dissolve metal. Your stomach lining survives because mucus keeps it off. "Mildly acidic" on a shampoo bottle, keeping a swimming pool at the right pH, why acid rain is a problem, hydrangeas changing colour with the pH of the soil - all of it sits on this scale.

Pour a great deal of water into an acid and the pH:
The lower the pH, the more there is of:

mix-2.title: Strong and weak acids do not differ by concentration
mix-2.lead: "Strong" and "concentrated" are different words. Mix them up and the whole of chemistry gets confusing.
mix-2.hook: Lesson 1 said pH is how many hydrogen ions there are. So to make an acid stronger, do you just add more? This is where a strong acid and a concentrated acid part company. They mean completely different things, and everyday speech calls both of them "a strong acid". You are going to see, grain by grain, why the same amount gives a different result.

predict.q: You prepare a strong acid and a weak acid at the same concentration. The strong one has a lower pH because:
opts: You put more of the strong one in
The strong acid splits into ions almost completely while the weak one splits only partly
The strong acid's molecules are heavier

missions: This is the Intro screen. Under Solution on the right, choose between Water · Strong Acid · Weak Acid · Strong Base · Weak Base.
Set Views at the bottom right to Particles. The grains inside the beaker appear.
Choose Strong Acid. What do the grains look like? Is there any HA left?
Switch to Weak Acid. Same concentration, and there are plenty of HA lumps left. That is the answer to ②.
Change Views to Graph. The vertical axis is a log scale in powers of ten. Compare the height of the H₃O⁺ bar for the strong and weak acids.
Drag the pH Color Key at the top left into the liquid and look at the colour. The strong and weak acids differ.
Dip the conductivity tester on the left into the liquid. The more ions there are, the brighter the bulb.
Compare the brightness for the strong and weak acids. Same concentration - why the difference?
Use the house button to reach the My Solution screen, where Initial Concentration and Strength can be set separately.
Leave the strength alone and raise the concentration. Then leave the concentration alone and raise the strength. The two handles do different jobs.
mix-2.record: What did the grains in the beaker look like for the strong and the weak acid at the same concentration? And what about the brightness of the bulb?

explain.body:
The answer is the strong one splits almost completely and the weak one only partly.

An acid put into water splits as HA → H⁺ + A⁻. That is ionisation, and the difference is how much of it splits.

  • Strong acid - nearly all of what you put in splits. Almost no HA lumps are left in the beaker.
  • Weak acid - only part of it splits. As you saw on screen, plenty of HA lumps remain.

So the same number of them going in gives a different number of H₃O⁺ coming out, and a different pH.

Two words are worth pinning down firmly here.

  • Strength (strong/weak) - how readily it splits. A property of the substance; you cannot change it.
  • Concentration (concentrated/dilute) - how much you put in. Yours to set.

So there is such a thing as a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid. Vinegar is a weak acid you can make concentrated; the hydrochloric acid in a lab is a strong acid you can dilute with plenty of water. This is what lesson 1 was showing when water never turned an acid into a base - the concentration changes and the strength does not.

The bulb was a good check. Electricity is carried by ions. The strong acid has plenty and glows bright; the weak one has few and glows dim. It turns an invisible degree of ionisation into brightness.

mix-2.real: Stomach acid (hydrochloric) is strong but very dilute. Vinegar (acetic acid) is weak but fairly concentrated. Which is why you can drink vinegar and dilute hydrochloric acid is dangerous. "pH neutral" on a detergent, why battery acid is hazardous, using lemon juice to kill the smell of fish - separate strength from concentration and it all makes sense.

quiz.q: What does the word strong acid mean?
opts: It splits into ions almost completely

quiz.q: What is left in quantity in a weak acid solution?
At the same concentration, which makes the bulb brighter?

mix-3.title: You may only touch the number in front
mix-3.lead: When you balance an equation you cannot turn H₂O into H₂O₂. That is a different substance altogether.
mix-3.hook: In a chemical reaction no atom is destroyed or created. They only change partners. So the left and right of an equation must have the same number of atoms. It is the same story as course 05, where adding the top and bottom numbers of a nuclear equation balanced on both sides. But when you set about matching the counts, your hand keeps reaching for the place you must not touch.

predict.q: You are balancing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. Changing the right side to H₂O₂ would make the oxygen count work. This approach is:
opts: Fine - the atom counts match, so no problem
Not allowed - H₂O₂ is not water but hydrogen peroxide, a different substance
Not allowed - it makes the arithmetic harder

missions: Start on the Intro screen. Choose between Make Ammonia · Separate Water · Combust Methane at the bottom.
Choose Separate Water. The boxes in front of each substance are what you can change.
Press View at the top right and choose the picture of the particles (the top item). Particles are drawn on both sides.
Raise and lower the numbers in the boxes while watching the balance in the middle. When the atom counts match on both sides, an = appears.
Look at the counts by element under the equation. It counts how many H and O there are on each side.
Confirm that the small number inside a formula (the 2 in H₂O) cannot be changed. That is the answer to ②.
Once it is right, Balanced appears at the top left.

Use the house button to reach the Equations screen for much harder ones. At the bottom you can choose Synthesis · Decomposition · Combustion.

mix-3.record: Write down the numbers you put in each box to balance the water equation. And which places could you change, and which could you not?

explain.body:
The answer is not allowed - H₂O₂ is a different substance. It is the commonest mistake in equations, and it is why the sim will not let you touch the small numbers at all.

The two numbers in a formula do completely different jobs.

  • The big number in front (the coefficient) - how many. 2 H₂O is two water molecules. You may change it.
  • The small number after (the subscript) - which substance. H₂O is water, H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide. Change it and you have a different substance.

Think of three bicycles against one tricycle. Either way there can be six wheels, but changing the number in front is "how many shall I fetch" while changing the object itself is "fetching something else entirely". Balancing an equation only ever lets you decide how many to use.

The answer for separating water is 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + 1 O₂. Left: 4 H and 2 O. Right: 4 H and 2 O.

Think back to course 05, where adding the top and bottom numbers of the alpha decay equation gave 211 = 207 + 4 and 84 = 82 + 2. There protons and neutrons were conserved; here atoms are. Different scale, same rule that nothing is lost and nothing is created.

mix-3.real: This rule is what lets a factory work out how much of each ingredient to put in. How many tonnes of nitrogen and hydrogen it takes to make a tonne of ammonia comes straight out of the equation. The mixture ratio of rocket fuel, the air-to-fuel ratio in a car engine, the chemistry inside a fire extinguisher - all of it rests on matching these counts.

mix-4.title: Whatever runs out first decides
mix-4.lead: However much bread you have, three slices of cheese means three sandwiches. Chemistry is exactly the same.
mix-4.hook: Lesson 3 had you matching the counts in an equation. But when you actually mix ingredients you almost never get them exactly right. One side is left over. So which side decides the result? This sim tells the chemistry story with sandwiches first. Once you know the answer it looks obvious, and yet written out as a chemical formula this same topic suddenly gets confusing.

predict.q: It takes 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese to make one sandwich. With 10 bread and 3 cheese, how many sandwiches?

missions: Start on the Sandwiches screen. At the top, choose between Cheese · Meat and Cheese · Custom.
Choose Cheese. The rule appears above: 2 bread + 1 cheese → 1 sandwich.
On the Before "Reaction" side below, set bread to 10 and cheese to 3.
Look at the After "Reaction" side. How many sandwiches were made? That is the answer to ②.
Look at the Leftovers box. What is left, and how much?
Raise the cheese one at a time. How far do the sandwiches climb before they stop?
Now raise the bread one at a time. With the cheese unchanged, do the sandwiches go up?
Use the house button to reach the Molecules screen, where the sandwiches turn into real chemical reactions.
Choose Make Water and put in different amounts of H₂ and O₂. It is the equation you balanced in lesson 3.
Try Make Ammonia and Combust Methane too, and see which ingredient runs out first.
mix-4.record: With 10 bread and 3 cheese, how many sandwiches and what was left over? And when did adding more H₂ in Make Water stop producing more water?

explain.body:
The answer is 3. There are 10 slices of bread but only 3 of cheese, so 3 sandwiches is the limit. 4 slices of bread are left, since 6 were used.

Out of that comes the rule that the result is decided not by the most plentiful ingredient but by the one that runs out first. Chemistry calls it the limiting reactant. Difficult name, sandwich meaning.

Which one runs out first cannot be told from the counts alone. There was more bread, at 10 slices, and the cheese still went first. You have to compare the ratio the rule demands against the ratio you have. Bread and cheese are needed 2 : 1, and you have 10 : 3 - for all that bread you would need 5 slices of cheese and you only have 3.

The ratios of lesson 11 apply here exactly. To double a recipe you have to double everything. Raise one side alone and that side is simply left over.

The Molecules screen is the same thing. Making water is 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, and if the O₂ is short, no amount of H₂ makes more water. The surplus H₂ just becomes leftovers.

Real reactions do work that way. However much you pour in, without a partner nothing reacts. Which is why a factory adds a little extra of the cheap ingredient so that none of the expensive one is left over.

mix-4.real: Cooking is the nearest example. Ten eggs and one cup of flour still only makes so many pancakes. A car engine mixing fuel and air at a set ratio, a rocket carrying both fuel and oxidiser, a battery going flat - all stories about whichever side runs out first.

mix-5.title: Measuring concentration by colour
mix-5.lead: The more concentrated it is, the more light it eats. The rule is exact enough that colour alone tells you the concentration.
mix-5.hook: Lesson 2 said concentration is "how much you put in". But once it has all dissolved, how do you measure it? The answer is colour. More concentrated eats more light, so measuring the light that gets through tells you the concentration backwards. But concentration is not the only thing that sets how much gets eaten. There is one more.

predict.q: Leaving the concentration alone, you double the width of the cell the light passes through. The absorbance (how much light is eaten) is:
opts: Unchanged - you did not touch the solution

missions: Start on the Concentration screen. Choose a substance under Solute on the right.
Pick something strongly coloured like Potassium permanganate and shake the shaker to put it in.
Dip the concentration probe on the left into the liquid. The deeper the colour, the bigger the number.
Pour in more water. The colour fades and the concentration number goes down.
Keep adding solute until Saturated! appears. That is the point where no more will dissolve.
Use the house button to reach the Beer's Law screen. The light is on the left, the cell of liquid in the middle, and the detector on the right.
Set the detector on the right to Absorbance. It reports how much light was eaten.
Double the Concentration handle below. How many times bigger is the absorbance?
Now leave the concentration alone and double the width of the cell (the handle in the middle). That is the answer to ②.
Switch to Transmittance. It moves the opposite way - the more is eaten, the less light gets through.
Change the Wavelength. The same solution absorbs very differently at different wavelengths.
mix-5.record: What happened to the absorbance when you doubled the concentration, and when you doubled the width of the cell?

explain.body:
The answer is doubled. The solution is untouched and the absorbance still rises.

The reason is simple. The path the light takes is twice as long, so it meets twice as many grains on the way. Each grain eats a little of the light, so meeting twice as many means twice as much eaten.

So two things set the absorbance.

  • Concentration - how densely packed the grains are along a given length
  • Width of the cell - how long a path the light travels

Both come down to changing the number of grains the light meets on its way, so they have the same effect. Written down, that is Beer's law, which the sim is named after.

In practice the important part is that one of the two has to be held fixed. To measure a concentration you must keep the width of the cell the same every time. Which is why laboratory cells (cuvettes) are made to a standard width of exactly 1 cm.

That the absorbance changed a great deal when you changed the wavelength matters too. Every substance has a colour it eats well. Purple potassium permanganate eats green light - it looks purple because it eats the green. What course 05 said about atoms absorbing only particular wavelengths turns practical here.

Transmittance is the other side of absorbance. Eat more and less gets through. The same fact seen from what was eaten or what is left.

mix-5.real: A hospital blood test is exactly this principle. A reagent produces a colour and the depth of that colour gives the amount of a component. Water quality testing, the dye content of food, how dark the line on a pregnancy test is, the colour change in a COVID test - devices that "measure an amount by depth of colour" are all around us.

fraction-1.title: Three pizzas shared between four people
fraction-1.lead: The line in a fraction is really a division sign. Here is how to answer 3 ÷ 4 without doing the division.
fraction-1.hook: Three pizzas shared equally between four people. One share is 0.75 of a pizza in decimals, but you can say the answer without dividing 3 by 4 at all. 3/4 of a pizza - that is the answer. The line in a fraction is not decoration; it is a division sign. And once you know that, something odd follows: the bigger the bottom number, the smaller the fraction.

predict.q: Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/8? Do not calculate - picture it.
opts: 1/3 - because fewer pieces means each piece is bigger
They are the same - the top numbers are both 1

missions: At the top centre of the screen, check that the shape chooser is on the circle. There are six: circle, horizontal bar, vertical bar, beaker, cake and number line.
At the middle right there is a large fraction. Set the denominator (the number under the line) to 3 and raise the numerator to 1. One circle splits into three pieces and one of them fills in.
Leave the numerator at 1 and raise the denominator alone to 8. Keep your eyes on the filled piece as it happens.
Flip the denominator between 3 and 8 a few times and compare the size of the piece. That is the answer to ②.
Now raise Max at the top right to 3. Three empty circles appear. Three pizzas.
Set the denominator to 4 and raise the numerator slowly from 1 to 12. At 12 the three circles are exactly full.
Change the shape chooser to the number line and see where the same fraction sits on it. A fraction is, in the end, a single number.
fraction-1.record: What happened to the size of the filled piece when you took the denominator from 3 to 8? And how many circles was 12/4?

explain.body:
The answer is 1/3. The denominator says how many pieces you cut the whole into. Cut it into 8 and each piece has to be thinner than if you cut it into 3.

If you said 1/8 was bigger, you compared 8 against 3 and nothing else. It is a very common mistake and a long-lasting one. A fraction is not two numbers but one value. Look at the top and bottom separately and you will get it wrong every time.

The numerator is how many of those pieces you have. So a bigger numerator makes it bigger and a bigger denominator makes it smaller. They pull opposite ways.

The sixth mission is the title of this lesson. At denominator 4 and numerator 12 the three circles filled exactly. So 12/4 = 3. Read backwards: three pizzas cut into quarters gives 12 pieces, three each - 3/4 of a pizza. That is what it means to say the line in a fraction is a division sign.

The number line makes it clearer still. 3/4 is a point between 0 and 1. Not a pizza, not a cake - just a number.

fraction-1.real: When a recipe says 3/4 cup it means "three of the four parts a cup divides into". A 3/8 inch spanner, a quarter note in music, a batting average - all of them say how many of the divided pieces you have. A calculator can tell you 0.375, but if you do not know what 3/8 means you cannot pick the right spanner.

fraction-2.title: Why multiplying works and adding does not
fraction-2.lead: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number and the value holds. So what about adding the same number? Almost everyone trips here.
fraction-2.hook: Multiply the top and bottom of 3/4 both by 2 and you get 6/8, with the value unchanged. That much you have been taught. Now add 2 to both the top and bottom of 3/4 and you get 5/6. You did the same thing to both - does the value hold this time too? There is a strong feeling that it should, because it was "fair". You are going to test that feeling.

predict.q: Add 2 to each of the numerator and denominator of 3/4 and you get 5/6. Compared with 3/4, 5/6 is:
opts: The same - you added the same to both

missions: At the bottom left set the denominator to 4 and the numerator to 3. 3/4 is drawn on the left.
Another fraction appears by itself to the right of the = in the middle. The green arrow beside it is the number you multiply by (1-3).
Raise the green arrow to 2. The right side becomes 6/8 and the shaded area is identical to the left. Check it with your eyes.
Take the green arrow up to 3. At 9/12 the area is still the same. The pieces have only been cut finer.
Now change the left side to 5/6 (denominator 6, numerator 5). Fix the shaded area in your mind.
Set it back to 3/4. Against 5/6, which was fuller? That is the answer to ②.
Change the chooser at the top right to the number line. Only the right side becomes a vertical number line. Move the green arrow between 1 and 3 and the marked point does not move up or down.
fraction-2.record: What happened to the shaded area as you took the green arrow to 2 and 3? And which was fuller, 3/4 or 5/6?

explain.body:
The answer is 5/6 is bigger. 3/4 is 0.75 and 5/6 is about 0.833. Adding the same number to top and bottom changes the value.

Why does multiplying work and adding not? Think about what happened on screen when you took the arrow to 2. The pieces were simply cut in half. Twice as many pieces and twice as many held, so the area is unchanged. Multiplying only changes how you cut, so the amount holds.

Adding is different. 3/4 → 5/6 does not cut the pieces; it builds a different fraction from scratch. The 2 added to the top and the 2 added to the bottom are 2s of different weight. Adding 2 to 3 nearly doubles it; adding 2 to 4 only gets you to 1.5 times. The top grows more, so the value rises.

Out of that comes a rule. When you put fractions over a common denominator or reduce them, you only ever multiply and divide. There is no adding or subtracting. That rule holds all the way to algebraic fractions with letters in them.

fraction-2.real: Map scales, photo aspect ratios, a 16:9 screen - all the same principle. Blowing 1920×1080 up to 3840×2160 does not change the shape of the picture because both sides were multiplied by 2. Add 100 to each side instead and the frame gets dragged toward a square and the picture distorts.

fraction-3.title: When the top is bigger than the bottom
fraction-3.lead: 8/3 is not a fraction written wrongly. It means two whole circles and a bit more.
fraction-3.hook: Learning fractions, they are always less than 1 - 1/2, 3/4 and so on. Then you meet one like 8/3 with the bigger number on top and your hand stops. It even looks like a mistake. It is not. You saw 12/4 = 3 in lesson 1, so you already have the answer.

predict.q: Written as a mixed number (a whole number plus a proper fraction), 8/3 is:

missions: In the large fraction at the middle right of the screen, set the denominator to 3 and the numerator to 8. Three circles appear and only the last one is short.
Count how many circles are full and how many pieces are in the last one.
Tick Mixed Number at the bottom right (just above the reset button). The large display changes to 2 and 2/3.
Open the Equation box at the bottom left. It writes out exactly how 8/3 was split up.
Raise the numerator by one to 9. The three circles fill and the display becomes 3. The fraction part disappears.
Raise the numerator slowly from 1 to 12 and watch when the display becomes a whole number. 3, 6, 9, 12 - there is a pattern.
Change the shape to the number line. You can see 8/3 sitting between 2 and 3. That is where the "2 and" of the mixed number comes from.
fraction-3.record: For 8/3, how many circles were full and how many pieces were left over? And which numerators made the display a whole number?

explain.body:
The answer is 2 and 2/3. Divide 8 by 3 and you get a quotient of 2 and a remainder of 2. The quotient is the whole part, the remainder is the numerator, and the denominator stays.

That division is exactly what you saw on screen. Fill circles cut into thirds with 8 pieces and two fill up and 2 pieces are left. 8 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 2. Lesson 1's "the line in a fraction is a division sign" is doing the work here.

If you chose 2 and 1/3, the remainder was probably miscounted. 3 × 2 = 6 and 8 − 6 = 2, so the remainder is 2.

The numerators that gave whole numbers - 3, 6, 9, 12 - are the same story. It comes out even only when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, because the remainder is 0.

The names are all you need to keep. Top-heavy like 8/3 is an improper fraction; with the whole number pulled out in front like 2 and 2/3 it is a mixed number. They are the same number written two ways. Neither is the right one - the mixed number is easier for judging size and the improper fraction is easier for calculating.

fraction-3.real: "1 and 1/2 cups of flour" in a recipe, "2 and 3/8 inches" in woodwork, "1 and 1/4 laps" running - everyday life uses mixed numbers, because 1 and 1/2 cups lands far faster than 3/2 cups. Calculators and computers do the opposite and convert everything to improper fractions, because multiplying and dividing gets much simpler.

fraction-4.title: Several ways to make the same fraction
fraction-4.lead: Being able to read one and being able to build one are different things. This time you assemble them by hand.
fraction-4.hook: So far you have been reading what the screen drew for you. Now you build them. You are given a target fraction and drag pieces in to fill it. And there is more than one way to fill it. Asked for 1/2 you can put down one half, or two quarter pieces. That is the whole of this lesson.

On the right are boxes with target fractions written on them. Drag pieces out of the tray below into the empty circle on the left.

fraction-4.record: How many 1/6 pieces did it take to fill 1/2? And write down two different ways you filled the same target.

explain.body:
The answer is 3. Three sixths is 3/6, and 3/6 has the same value as 1/2. Lesson 2's "multiply the top and bottom by the same number" gets built by hand here, since multiplying 1/2 top and bottom by 3 gives 3/6.

If you answered 2, you may have paired the denominator 6 with two pieces. Two pieces of a sixth is 2/6, which is 1/3, and that falls short of a half.

The real lesson of this game is that there are several right answers. A half is made by one half, by two quarters, by three sixths, by four eighths. There are endlessly many fractions of the same value, and the simplest form among them is 1/2. Finding that simplest form is what reducing a fraction is.

The number card levels (the bottom row) are a little different. With no picture, you choose the numbers to put in the numerator and denominator yourself. It feels much harder because you have to build it in your head instead of leaning on the picture, and that is exactly the step to be taking now.

A wrong group simply comes back. No points lost, no lives. It is built that way so you will try things freely.

fraction-4.real: Think of Lego. An eight-stud space takes two four-stud bricks or four two-stud bricks. A carpenter needing 3/4 inch using six 1/8 inch shims, a cook measuring a cup with a quarter-cup measure - the same thing. The pieces can be any size as long as the amount they add to is the same.

fraction-5.lead: Pictures and numbers, improper fractions and mixed numbers - find the same number among the different faces. The close of four lessons.
fraction-5.hook: By now you have all the tools. A fraction is a division (lesson 1), multiplying top and bottom by the same number holds the value (lesson 2), a top-heavy one can become a mixed number (lesson 3), and there are several ways to make the same fraction (lesson 4). The answer is 4/5. 3/4 is 0.75 and 4/5 is 0.8 - different numbers. It looks the same because top and bottom each went up by one, but as lesson 2 showed, adding does not hold the value.

The other three are all 3/4. 6/8 is top and bottom times 2, 9/12 is times 3, and the circle cut into eighths with 6 shaded is 6/8 drawn as a picture.

What this game is after is the habit of reducing before you compare. To see whether two fractions are equal, put each in its simplest form and set them side by side. 6/8 → 3/4, 9/12 → 3/4, 4/5 → 4/5. It separates at a glance.

The balance is not decoration. When you are wrong it tells you which side is bigger as well. That is more useful than getting it right, because it tells you why you were wrong. Which is why a mission asks you to get one wrong on purpose.

The scoring - 2 points first time, 1 point second - has a point too. It is built so that getting it right first time pays better than guessing. Do not rush the cards up; reduce them in your head first.

ratio-1.title: Adding does not keep a ratio
ratio-1.lead: Add 2 to each of 2 and 3 and you get 4 and 5. That is no longer the same ratio.
ratio-1.hook: Two packets of noodles take 3 cups of water. So how much water for four packets? Your hand goes two ways here. "Two more packets, so two more cups - 5 cups" is one; "twice the noodles, so twice the water - 6 cups" is the other. One is right and one is wrong, and the wrong one feels more natural. This sim shows you the difference with your eyes and your ears, through the height of two hands.

Choose Challenge 1 on the right. That fixes the ratio you have to hit.
Drag the two hands. When the ratio is right the background deepens and the sound changes. You can tell without looking at any numbers.

ratio-1.record: From left 2 and right 3, when you raised the left alone to 4, what did the right have to be for the background to deepen again?

explain.body:
The answer is 6. The left hand doubled from 2 to 4, so the right hand has to double from 3 to 6.

If you chose 5, you were trying to match by adding - the left went up 2, so the right goes up 2. A very natural thought, and therefore a very common mistake. But 4 : 5 is a different ratio from 2 : 3.

Why does adding fail? A ratio says how many times one is the other. 2 : 3 means "the right is 1.5 times the left". 4 : 6 is also 1.5 times. But 4 : 5 is 1.25 - the relationship has changed.

It is exactly the story from course 10 (fractions), where multiplying top and bottom by the same number holds the value and adding does not. It is the same thing as 2/3 and 4/6 being equal while 4/5 is not. A ratio and a fraction are really the same object.

That the ratio held when you raised both hands together matters too. 2 : 3, 4 : 6 and 6 : 9 are all the same ratio, and the actual size can be anything at all. A ratio is a relationship, not a size.

ratio-1.real: Recipes are the commonest example. Going from two servings to four means doubling every ingredient; adding "a bit more" of everything wrecks the taste. Enlarging a photo without distortion by multiplying both sides by the same number, a map scale, a 16:9 screen - all on the same rule.

explain.body:
The answer is exactly the same purple. There is three times as much of it, but the relationship between red and blue is unchanged. 1 : 2 and 3 : 6 both say "twice as much blue as red".

If you chose "three times deeper", you mixed up amount and ratio. Pouring three times the paint makes more of it, not a deeper version of it. To change the shade you have to change the ratio itself, which is why 2 : 6 looked so different.

That is the message of the whole sim. A ratio decides the result regardless of size.

  • Paint - the ratio sets the colour. The amount only sets how much you make.
  • Necklace - the bead ratio sets the pattern. A longer necklace has the same pattern.
  • Billiard table - the length-to-width ratio sets the shape of the path. Scale it up and the path is similar.
  • Apples - the ratio of count to cost sets the cost per apple.

The path staying the same when you doubled both sides of the billiard table is a particularly good check. It is the story from course 10, lesson 2, where doubling a screen resolution did not change the shape of the picture. Multiply both by the same number and the relationship holds.

That last apples screen is where the next lesson starts. Ten apples for five dollars - what is one apple? That is a unit rate.

ratio-2.real: A paint shop mixing a colour uses exactly this. One litre or twenty, the same ratio gives the same colour. Coffee grounds to water, a cement mix, camera exposure settings - all "not the amount, the ratio".

ratio-3.title: Which one is actually cheaper
ratio-3.lead: Six for $3 and ten for $4.50. To compare two things that differ in both, you have to bring them onto one measure.
ratio-3.hook: The same fruit is sold two ways at the supermarket. Six for $3 and ten for $4.50. Which is the better buy? At a glance $3 is cheaper, and by count ten is more. Both are true and neither gives you an answer. To compare things that will not compare, you have to put them on one measure. That measure is what one costs.

predict.q: Apples are 6 for $3 in one bag and 10 for $4.50 in another. Which is cheaper per apple?
opts: You cannot compare them with different counts

missions: Start on the Shopping screen. Choose an item on the left - Apples, Lemons, Carrots, candy and so on.
Put things on the scale in the middle, or set the Cost, and two lines are drawn side by side on the Double Number Line above. The top is dollars and the bottom is the count.
Look at the Unit Rate? line in the Questions box on the right. It tells you what one costs. The key number of this sim.
Raise the count 1 → 2 → 3. The two lines grow in step. That is what the same ratio looks like.
Open the rest of the Questions box. Problems like "Cost of 10 Apples?" appear.
Answer one and then check it using the double number line. You can read the answer off the line instead of calculating it.
Change items and note the unit rate of each, then compare which is cheaper. That is how you settle ②.
Use the house button to reach the Shopping Lab, where you set the prices and make your own problems.
On the Racing Lab the quantities are time and distance instead of money. The unit rate becomes speed.
ratio-3.record: Write down the unit rate (cost per item) for two of the items you chose. And which was the better buy?

explain.body:
The answer is the 10 for $4.50.

  • 6 for $3 → 3 ÷ 6 = $0.50 each
  • 10 for $4.50 → 4.50 ÷ 10 = $0.45 each

Look only at the total and $3 seems cheaper; look only at the count and ten seems better. Both look at one side only. The moment you convert to cost per item you can measure the two bags with the same ruler.

A ratio with the base set to 1 like that is a unit rate. Why 1? Because from 1 you only have to multiply. Knowing one apple is 45 cents, seven apples is 45 × 7 and twenty-three is 45 × 23, straight off.

The double number line on screen draws that. The top line is cost and the bottom is count, and the two grow in step. In step is exactly what the same ratio means, which is why knowing one side lets you read the other off without calculating.

The Racing Lab is the same object. Distance ÷ time is how far in one second, which is speed. 60 mph, 15 km per litre, calories per 100 g - an enormous number of everyday figures are unit rates.

ratio-3.real: The small price per 100 g on a supermarket shelf label is exactly this. Pack sizes vary so wildly that nothing else compares, which is why the law requires the unit price alongside. Price per GB on a phone tariff, a car's fuel economy, an hourly wage - all figures with the base set to 1.

At 45 cents each, seven cost:
Why is the base of a unit rate set to 1?
opts: Because you can then get any count by multiplying

ratio-4.title: A mean is what you get sharing it out evenly
ratio-4.lead: Not the formula for a mean but what a mean is. Let the water flow and it appears by itself.
ratio-4.hook: A mean is taught as "add them all up and divide by how many". You memorised the formula, but what it means stays hazy. This sim connects cups with pipes. The water flows on its own until every cup is at the same level, and that level is the mean. You have made a mean without using the formula.

predict.q: Three cups hold 2 · 4 · 6 of water. Open the pipes and let it spread evenly. The level in each cup is:

missions: Start on the Level Out screen. Set Number of Cups at the bottom to 3.
Drag the handle under each cup to set the water levels to 2 · 4 · 6.
Open the pipes in the middle. The water flows until every cup is at the same level. What level? That is the answer to ②.
Close the pipes and push one cup right up. Open them again - what is the new level?
Turn on Predict Mean on the right and mark your own guess before you open the pipes.
Turn on Tick Marks and your guess leaves a mark to compare against the answer.
Take the cups up to 7, fill them unevenly and open the pipes. More cups, same thing.
Use the house button to reach the Fair Share screen. This time it is apples being shared among people, not water.
Press Share and the apples divide evenly. When they will not divide exactly they split into pieces - the fractions of course 10 turning up here.
On the Balance Point screen the mean appears as the place a see-saw balances. Another face of the same mean.
ratio-4.record: What level did 2 · 4 · 6 come to when you opened the pipes? And what happened when the apples would not divide exactly?

explain.body:
The answer is 4. (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 4. But what matters is not the arithmetic - it is what actually happened on screen.

No water arrived and none disappeared. The water that was there was simply spread out evenly. So the meaning of a mean is this - "gather it all and share it equally; how much is one share?"

That is also where the shape of the formula comes from. Adding them all is pouring the water into one tank; dividing by how many is pouring it back equally into the cups. The formula just writes down those two actions.

If you chose 3, you picked the middle value. With 2 · 4 · 6 the median happens to be 4 as well so it would not have caught you out, but for 2 · 3 · 10 the median is 3 and the mean is 5. That is the difference course 14 takes up.

The apples splitting into pieces on the Fair Share screen matters too. Seven apples between three people is 2 and 1/3 each. Course 10's "the line in a fraction is a division sign" is doing the work again. A mean is a division, and a division can come out as a fraction.

The Balance Point screen shows the same mean in a completely different way. Put the values on a see-saw and the mean is the fulcrum where it balances. So one very large value at one end drags the fulcrum toward it - the whole reason a mean is vulnerable to outliers is in that picture.

ratio-4.real: "Average temperature this month", "class average", "income per head" - all of them are "gather it all and share it equally". Income per head being high while nobody feels it is because the water was not really spread out; it was spread out only in the arithmetic. Which is why a mean should always be read alongside "how evenly is it spread".

graph-1.title: Putting a number on "steep"
graph-1.lead: How to turn "that hill is steep" into a single number. That number is the slope.
graph-1.hook: Maps mark walking routes with figures like a 12% gradient. Roofs have one, road signs have one, wheelchair ramp regulations have one. It turns the feeling of "steep" into a single number. Look at how that number is made and it is one division. And a great many people memorise which is divided by which the wrong way round.

predict.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 2) and (3, 8)?

missions: Start on the Slope screen. The graph is on the left and the slope equation is at the top right.
Drag the two points on the graph. The numbers in the equation follow.
Check that the equation is the vertical difference over the horizontal difference. Vertical on top, horizontal below.
Set the points to (1, 2) and (3, 8). The value you get is the answer to ②.
Now move the points so the line runs down to the right. The slope goes negative.
Make the line completely horizontal. The slope is 0. Now stand it vertical - what does it say?
Keep a line you like with Save Line, then build a line with a different slope and compare them side by side.
Use the house button to visit the Point-Slope screen. One point and a slope fix a line uniquely.
(The Slope-Intercept screen is lesson 2. You can skip it for now.)
graph-1.record: What value did the slope take when you ran the line down to the right? And what did it say when you stood the line vertical?

explain.body:
The answer is 3. It climbs 6 vertically (2 to 8) while going 2 horizontally (1 to 3), so 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

If you chose 1/3 you had it upside down. Very common. There is only one way to remember it - slope is "how far up" divided by "how far along". Think of a hill and it will not slip. Walk a little and climb a lot and it is steep, and steep has to be a big number.

Collecting what you confirmed on screen:

  • A line going up to the right → slope positive
  • A line going down to the right → slope negative
  • A horizontal line → slope 0 (walk as far as you like and you never climb)
  • A vertical line → slope undefined (you went 0 horizontally, so you would divide by 0)

That the screen answers "undefined" for a vertical line matters. It is not that the slope is infinite or very large - dividing by 0 means there is no value at all.

Remember what the Point-Slope screen showed too. One point and a slope fix a line uniquely. Put the other way round, it takes exactly two pieces of information to fix a line. y = mx + b in lesson 2 is exactly those two pieces.

graph-1.real: A 12% gradient is a slope of 0.12 - you climb 12 m over 100 m travelled. A wheelchair ramp is required by law to be 1/12 or less, and roofs are built steeper where the snow is heavy. "The slope has turned" on a stock chart, the elevation graph on a cycling app - all the same single division.

quiz.q: The slope of the line through (0, 5) and (4, 1) is:
A line with slope 0 is:
The slope of a vertical line is:
opts: Undefined - it would mean dividing by 0

graph-2.title: Two numbers fix a line
graph-2.lead: y = mx + b. The two letters do different jobs. Mix them up and you will always be wrong.
graph-2.hook: Lesson 1 said it takes two pieces of information to fix a line. Naming those two pieces gives you y = mx + b. m is the slope and b is the height where it meets the y axis. That much you can memorise. The problem is what the line does when you change only one of them. That is where it splits.

predict.q: In y = 2x + 3, you change the 3 to a 5. The line:
opts: Keeps its shape and moves up by 2

missions: On the Slope-Intercept screen, check that the equation at the top right is in the form y = m x + b.
Set the equation to y = 2x + 3 and fix the current line in your mind.
Raise b alone from 3 to 5. Does the steepness change, or does the whole thing move? That is the answer to ②.
Now leave b alone and raise m from 2 to 4. What changes this time?
Keep the current line with Save Line and change m to −2. Compare it against the saved line.
Set b to 0 and the line passes through the origin. That is where you see b is the height at which it meets the y axis.
Drag the line itself on the graph. The numbers in the equation follow. It works in both directions.
Use the house button to reach the Line Game and start at Level 1. You name the equation from the picture, or draw the line from the equation.
Move up to Level 3 or above. It starts giving you two points and asking for the equation.
graph-2.record: Write one line each on what the line did when you changed b alone and when you changed m alone.

explain.body:
The answer is it keeps its shape and moves up by 2. b does not touch the steepness. It just slides the whole line up or down.

Why? Change the 3 in y = 2x + 3 to a 5 and the y value goes up by 2 at every x. Whether x is 0 or 100, it rises by 2, so every point on the line lifts by 2 in parallel. Rising in parallel leaves the slope unchanged.

m is different. Change m from 2 to 4 and a step of 1 in x raises y by 4 instead of 2. How much it rises now depends on x, so the line rotates about one point. That point is where it crosses the y axis - there x is 0, so mx is 0 however much you change m.

To collect it:

  • Change b → the line slides up and down (slope unchanged)
  • Change m → the line turns about the y-intercept (height unchanged)

That the two do not interfere with each other is the reason y = mx + b is the form we use. You can set each one separately.

There is a reason the Line Game gives you two points from level 3. As lesson 1 confirmed, two points give you the slope, and a slope with one point gives you b. Both pieces get filled in.

graph-2.real: A taxi fare is exactly this shape. The flag fall is b and the charge per mile is m. A phone tariff, a gym joining fee plus a monthly fee, a delivery charge plus the food - all the same. Comparing two tariffs by asking "how much use before the other one is cheaper" is finding where two lines cross.

Change y = x + 4 into y = x − 2 and the line:
Which point does not move when you change m?
opts: Where it crosses the y axis
Where it crosses the x axis

graph-3.title: A minus sign that moves it right
graph-3.lead: Leave straight lines behind and you get a parabola. And there is one trap in it where the sign looks backwards.
graph-3.hook: The lines in lessons 1 and 2 were all straight, because all that was attached to x was a single x. Bring in x² and the line curves into a parabola - the path of a thrown ball, the jet of a fountain, the cross section of a satellite dish. But the formula for moving a parabola about contains a trap that catches almost everyone once. A minus sign moves it to the right.

predict.q: Where is the vertex of y = (x − 3)²?

missions: Start on the Explore screen. At the top right are y = a x² + b x + c and three sliders.
Move a alone. What happens to the width from 1 to 3? And down at 0.2?
Take a negative. The parabola flips over.
Take a to 0. The x² disappears and you get a straight line - back to lessons 1 and 2.
Turn on the Quadratic Terms and Equations checkboxes at the bottom right. You can see which part of the formula does which part of the graph.
Use the house button to reach the Vertex Form screen. The formula becomes y = a(x − h)² + k.
Turn on the Vertex checkbox. A point marks the vertex.
Set h to 3 with a at 1 and k at 0, giving y = (x − 3)². Where did the vertex go? That is the answer to ②.
Set h to −3 and check the vertex goes the other way.
Move k. This one moves up and down with the sign as written.
Turn on the Axis of Symmetry checkbox. A vertical line through the vertex appears.
graph-3.record: What happened to the width when you raised and lowered a? And what was the x coordinate of the vertex when you set h to 3?

explain.body:
The answer is (3, 0). You subtract and it goes right. The sign looks backwards.

The reason is simple. The vertex is where the bracket becomes 0. (x − 3)² is smallest when the square is 0, and x − 3 = 0 needs x = 3. So the vertex has an x coordinate of 3.

Remember it this way and it will not confuse you - find the x that makes the bracket 0. For (x + 5)² it is x = −5; for (x − 7)² it is x = 7.

k, by contrast, moves with its sign. y = (x − 3)² + 2 has its vertex at (3, 2). Only h is backwards, and k is honest, because h is attached to the x side and k is added on the y side. k is doing exactly what b did in lesson 2 when raising it lifted the line.

Let us collect what a showed you.

  • Large |a| → narrower (y jumps further at the same x, so it is steeper)
  • Small |a| → wider
  • Negative a → flipped over
  • a = 0 → not a parabola but a straight line

That raising a makes it narrower is especially confusing, because "bigger should mean bigger" says otherwise. What gets bigger is the height, and seen from the side that makes it look thinner.

graph-3.real: Satellite dishes and car headlights have parabolic cross sections because of the way they gather to one point (the focus). The arc of a basketball shot, a fountain jet and the cables of a bridge are close to parabolas too. Tweaking a jump curve when making a game comes down to adjusting a and k.

graph-4.title: A slope can be a graph too
graph-4.lead: A curve has a different slope in every place. Collect those slopes and draw them and you get a new graph.
graph-4.hook: The straight line in lesson 1 had the same slope wherever you measured, so its slope was one number and that was that. The parabola in lesson 3 is different. The left flank goes down and the right flank goes up, so the slope differs from place to place. Which suggests something: measure the slope at every place and draw those values as a graph of their own. This sim does it live.

predict.q: Draw the "slope at every place" of the straight line y = 2x as a graph. What do you get?
opts: A steeper line through the origin

missions: The screen is split into two panels. The top is the original curve f(x) and the bottom is the slope graph.
Among the shape buttons on the right (hill, pedestal, tilt, shift), choose tilt and drag in the top panel to make a straight slope.
With a straight slope, check that the bottom panel is a horizontal line. That is the answer to ②.
Drag the slope steeper. The height of the horizontal line below rises with it.
Tilt the slope the other way. The line below drops below 0.
Now choose the hill shape and draw a hill in the top panel. What shape does the graph below become?
Turn on the Tangent checkbox on the right. A tangent line appears in the top panel and the vertical gauge at the left edge gives the slope at that place.
Drag the tangent to the top of the hill. The slope becomes 0, and the graph below passes through 0 at that place.
Check that the graph below is above 0 on the uphill and below 0 on the downhill.
Turn on the Reference Line on the right and drag it left and right to compare the two graphs at the same x.
graph-4.record: What shape was the graph below when you drew a straight slope? And what was its value at the top of the hill?

explain.body:
The answer is a horizontal line at height 2.

The line y = 2x has a slope of 2 wherever you measure it. At x = −5, at 0, at 100 - always 2. So drawing "the slope at every place" as a graph gives you a graph whose value is 2 everywhere, which is a horizontal line at height 2.

If you chose "the same line", you were overlaying the original graph and the slope graph. They draw completely different things. The vertical axis of the top graph is height; the vertical axis of the bottom one is slope.

What the hill showed you is the heart of this lesson.

  • Uphill (rising) → slope positive → the graph below is above 0
  • The top (flat for an instant) → slope 0 → the graph below passes through 0
  • Downhill → slope negative → the graph below is below 0

So finding where the graph below crosses 0 is finding a peak or a valley in the graph above. You can find the highest point without looking at the graph at all. That is the commonest reason calculus gets used.

At school the graph below is called the derivative and written f′(x). You do not need the name yet. It is enough to keep the picture of a graph made by collecting the slopes.

graph-4.real: A car dashboard is exactly this relationship. If the odometer is the top graph, the speedometer is the bottom one - speed is "how fast the distance is growing", the slope of the distance graph. An ECG, the rate of change of a share price, and "the rise is levelling off" on an epidemic curve all mean the bottom graph has started to come down.

quiz.q: The slope graph of the horizontal line y = 5 is:
opts: A horizontal line at height 0 (the x axis)

quiz.q: Where the slope graph below crosses 0, the graph above is:
opts: At a peak or a valley

life-1.title: A rabbit does not change; the population does
life-1.lead: A white rabbit does not turn brown on brown ground. The brown ones simply survive more often.
life-1.hook: Snowy ground has more white rabbits and bare earth has more brown ones. People usually say the rabbits "changed to suit the environment", as though a rabbit looked around and altered its colour. But a single rabbit never changes colour in its life. So what did change? This sim runs a population of rabbits through generations and shows you.

predict.q: Brown ground with wolves about. A brown mutation appears in a population of white rabbits. After many generations:
opts: White rabbits turn brown as they grow

missions: Start on the Intro screen. Press Add a Mate in the middle to let the rabbits breed.
Watch for a moment and the rabbits multiply exponentially. The generation count climbs.
Under Add Mutation on the right, choose Fur and add Brown Fur as Dominant.
Choose Population on the graph at the left and turn on the White Fur and Brown Fur lines. Both climb together.
There are no wolves yet, so neither has an advantage. Check that the proportion stays about the same.
Now turn on Wolves under Environmental Factors on the right. What happens? That is the answer to ②.
Change the graph to Proportions. The share held by white and brown rabbits is clear at a glance.
Watch to see whether any individual rabbit changes colour. Does a white rabbit turn brown, or does it simply disappear?
Now change the background to snow (the environment can be chosen on the Lab screen). Which one has the advantage now?
Turn on Limited Food and add a Teeth mutation. Under a different pressure, a different trait wins.
Turn on the Pedigree graph to see how one rabbit's descendants spread.
life-1.record: How did the proportions of white and brown rabbits differ before and after you turned the wolves on? And did you ever see an individual rabbit change colour?

explain.body:
The answer is the proportion of brown rabbits rises. No individual rabbit changes colour. You will never have seen a white rabbit turn brown on screen.

What actually happened is this.

  • Brown rabbits are harder to spot on brown ground, so they are more likely to survive.
  • Survivors have young, so the brown gene gets passed on more often.
  • Generation by generation, brown takes a larger share of the population.

So what changes is not the individual but the make-up of the population. That is natural selection, and it is where it parts company most sharply with the common belief. Not "giraffes stretched their necks" but "long-necked giraffes survived better".

It also matters that both of two things are needed.

  • Variation - there have to be differences in the population already. Mutation supplies them.
  • Selection pressure - something has to decide which is favoured. The wolves play that part.

Before the wolves the proportions barely moved. Variation without pressure has no direction. Conversely, pressure without variation leaves nothing to select from, and the whole population can disappear.

Remember, too, that the advantage flipped when you changed the background to snow. Brown is not the "better" trait. The environment decides what counts as better. Change the environment and the answer changes.

life-1.real: Antibiotic resistance is exactly this story. Bacteria that survive the antibiotic breed and the resistant share rises - the bacteria did not "build up resistance"; the resistant ones that were already there survived. Pesticide-resistant insects, the spread of a COVID variant and crop breeding all work the same way.

quiz.q: In natural selection, what changes?
opts: The proportions of traits in the population

quiz.q: Natural selection needs both of:
On snow, white fur has the advantage. That means:
opts: White fur is the better trait
The environment decides what is favoured

life-2.title: A cell membrane does not let just anything through
life-2.lead: Oxygen goes straight through. Sodium needs a door. Without a door it does not get in however much of it there is.
life-2.hook: Lesson 1 looked at a population of rabbits; this time the scale narrows right down to a single cell. A cell is wrapped in a membrane, and to stay alive it has to let in what it needs and put out what it does not. But this membrane does not sieve by size like a strainer. Some things pass straight through and some only get through a door.

predict.q: There is plenty of sodium (Na⁺) outside the cell and almost none inside. Will the sodium get in by itself?
opts: Yes - it flows from where there is more to where there is less
No - it cannot pass the membrane and needs a channel

missions: Start on the Simple Diffusion screen. The horizontal line across the middle is the membrane: Outside above, Inside below.
In the Solute Concentrations panel below, choose O₂ and put plenty of it outside the cell only.
Watch for a moment. Does the oxygen go straight through the membrane?
Leave it until the oxygen is about the same on both sides. That is the end of diffusion, or equilibrium.
Now put plenty of Na⁺ outside the cell only. Does the same thing happen as with oxygen? That is the answer to ②.
Try Glucose the same way. What about a big, heavy molecule?
Turn on Crossing Highlights on the right and the moment of crossing flashes.
Use the house button to reach the Facilitated Diffusion screen, where you can drag transport proteins into the empty slots along the top.
Put a sodium channel in and add sodium again. Does it get through this time?
Even with a channel, which way does it flow? From more to less?
Go to the Active Transport screen and fit a pump. This time it pushes from less to more. It spends energy to do it.
life-2.record: Note whether oxygen, sodium and glucose each went straight through the membrane. And which way did the sodium flow once you fitted a channel?

explain.body:
The answer is no. However much of it there is outside, sodium cannot get past the membrane without a channel.

A cell membrane is a thin layer of fatty material, so what gets through is decided by size and character.

  • Small and electrically neutral (O₂, CO₂) - goes straight through.
  • Charged ions (Na⁺, K⁺) - cannot get through the fatty layer. Needs a channel.
  • Big, heavy molecules (glucose) - also needs a channel.

That is why a membrane is called selectively permeable. It does not just sieve by size; it chooses what to let in.

That the sodium flowed from more to less once you fitted a channel matters too. A channel only opens a door; the direction is still set by concentration. That is facilitated diffusion - it helps, but it cannot go against the flow.

Active transport is genuinely different. A pump pushes from less to more. Water does not run uphill by itself, and neither does this - it is not free. The cell has to spend energy.

Why bother? Because a cell has to keep the concentrations inside and outside deliberately different. That difference makes nerve signals and draws nutrients in. Left alone everything equalises, so being alive is a matter of standing against equilibrium.

The concentration of course 09 is used exactly as it stands. The difference is that there it was one beaker and here it is two rooms divided by a membrane.

life-2.real: A nerve sending a signal is a matter of sodium and potassium concentration differences. A large part of the energy your body uses goes into running those pumps. Getting the concentration of a drip exactly right, kidneys filtering out only the waste, vegetables pickling in brine - all stories about membranes and concentrations.

quiz.q: Which of these can go straight through a cell membrane?
In facilitated diffusion, which way does a substance flow?
How does active transport differ from diffusion?
opts: It spends energy to move against the concentration

life-3.title: What comes in has to go out for the temperature to hold
life-3.lead: Raise the greenhouse gases and does the energy the Earth sends to space go down? The answer is "for a while".
life-3.hook: Lesson 2 said a cell keeps inside and outside different by standing against equilibrium. The Earth is solving a similar problem. Energy comes in from the Sun and goes out to space, and as much out as in holds the temperature steady. So what if you raise the greenhouse gases and block the way out? Does the Earth simply keep getting hotter? This sim has an Energy Balance panel so you can see the answer for yourself.

predict.q: You raise the greenhouse gas concentration sharply. What eventually happens to the energy the Earth sends to space?
opts: It dips for a while, then as the Earth warms it matches what comes in again

missions: Start on the Waves screen. Tick Energy Balance at the bottom right of the view, and In · Out · Net bars appear at the top left.
Press Start Sunlight in the middle to switch the sunlight on.
Set the Greenhouse Gas Concentration on the right to None and wait. Net goes to 0 and the temperature settles. Write that temperature down.
Now push the concentration sharply toward Lots. What happens to the Out bar?
Look at the Net bar. It is no longer 0 and the temperature starts to rise.
Leave it running a good while. The temperature rises and then stops. What is Net then? That is the answer to ②.
Note the new temperature and compare it against the first.
Watch where the Infrared waves turn back on screen. Greenhouse gases let the sunlight through and catch only the infrared.
Under Energy on the right, switch between Sunlight and Infrared and compare the lengths of the two waves.
Turn on the Cloud. A cloud turns sunlight back - the opposite direction to a greenhouse gas.

Below the Greenhouse Gas Concentration box on the right are two buttons with no words. Press the right-hand one (the calendar picture, for choosing by period) and work through Ice Age · 1750 · 1950 · 2020, noting the temperature.
Use the house button to reach the Photons screen to see the same thing grain by grain.
life-3.record: Write down the settled temperature with no greenhouse gas and with plenty of it. And what was the Net bar once the temperature had settled?

explain.body:
The answer is it dips for a while and then matches what comes in again. On screen the Net bar will have come back to 0.

Follow it through.

  • Raise the greenhouse gases and more infrared is caught, so Out falls.
  • In is unchanged and Out has fallen, so Net goes positive and energy piles up on Earth.
  • Piling up means the temperature rises.
  • But a hotter object gives off more infrared. So Out climbs back up.
  • Eventually In = Out again, at a higher temperature.

So what greenhouse gases do is not heat the Earth forever but raise the temperature at which the balance settles. Pile on a thicker duvet and your temperature does not climb without limit; you settle warmer.

What matters is that this change of temperature is not free. Energy accumulates on the way to the new balance, and while it does, ice melts and the sea expands.

That greenhouse gases catch only infrared is central too. They let sunlight through and catch only the infrared the Earth radiates back. Course 05, lesson 3 said each atom absorbs particular wavelengths, and here it is on a planetary scale. Course 09, lesson 5 said each substance has a colour it eats well - the same story.

The cloud worked the other way. It turns sunlight back and reduces In. Which is part of why climate is hard to predict - the warming and the cooling move together.

If you noted the temperatures by period, the change after 1750 will have stood out. That is the industrial revolution.

life-3.real: Venus is the useful comparison. It is only the second planet out, yet its surface is 460 °C - hotter than Mercury. Its atmosphere is 96% carbon dioxide, so the greenhouse effect is extreme. The Moon, with no atmosphere at all, swings between 120 °C by day and −170 °C by night. The duvet of an atmosphere is what makes Earth liveable.
